lessons.title: What Is the MERN Stack? How a Web Request Travels
lessons.description: What MongoDB, Express, React and Node.js each do, how they fit together, and a script that follows one request from browser to database and back.

content.text: The MERN stack is a popular way to build a complete web application using one language, JavaScript, from the screen the visitor sees to the database that keeps the data. The four letters are four tools: **M**ongoDB, **E**xpress, **R**eact and **N**ode.js. In this course you will use all four to build a real application, a job tracker where a person signs in, adds the jobs they applied for, searches and filters them, attaches the resume they sent, and sees simple numbers about their search. At the end you will put it on a server on the internet.

You do not need to know any of the four tools yet. You do need to be able to read basic JavaScript: variables, functions and objects. The next three lessons refresh the parts of modern JavaScript that every MERN app uses, so if you are rusty, you are in the right place. Every lesson comes with the exact source code for that point in the project, as a zip you can download from the top of the lesson, so you can always compare your work with a working copy.
The four parts and what each one is for

items: **React** runs in the visitor's browser. It draws the screens: lists, forms, buttons. It does not store anything permanently, because everything in the browser can be closed, cleared or changed by the visitor.
**Node.js** is JavaScript running on a server, outside the browser. It is the engine that runs your back end code.
**Express** is a small library that sits on top of Node.js. It receives requests such as “give me my jobs” and lets you write the code that answers them. A group of such answers is called an **API**.
**MongoDB** is the database. It keeps the information safely on disk: people, jobs, notes. The server asks it for data and tells it what to save.

content.text: People often call React the **front end** and Node.js with Express the **back end**. The database is a third layer behind the back end. The important rule is this: the browser never talks to the database directly. It talks to your API, and your API talks to the database. That gap is where you check who the person is, what they are allowed to do, and whether the data they sent makes sense.
The journey of one request
Suppose a signed-in person opens the “My jobs” page. Here is what happens, step by step.

items: The browser loads the React app, which is just JavaScript, HTML and CSS files. React draws the page frame and shows “Loading…”.
React calls `fetch('/api/jobs')`. This is an **HTTP request**: a message with a method (`GET`), a path (`/api/jobs`) and some headers, one of which says who is asking.
The request travels over the internet to your server, where Node.js is listening. Express looks at the method and path and picks the matching route.
The route checks the headers, finds the person, and asks MongoDB: “find the jobs that belong to this person”.
MongoDB returns the documents. Express turns them into **JSON**, a text format both sides understand, and sends an **HTTP response** with a status code such as `200`.
React receives the JSON, saves it in its state, and draws one card for every job. Loading is gone, jobs are on the screen.

content.text: Every feature in this course is a variation on this journey. Adding a job sends data the other way. Signing in sends an email and a password and gets back a token. Uploading a resume sends a file. Once the journey is clear in your head, MERN stops looking like four separate technologies and becomes one idea repeated.
See it run: a request in 40 lines

Before installing anything, run this script. It uses only Node.js. It plays all three roles: a “database” (an array), a “server” (Node's built-in `http` module) and a “browser” (the built-in `fetch`). Each one prints what it is doing, so you can read the journey in your terminal.

The output follows the same order as the list above: the browser calls, the server receives, the database answers, the server replies, the browser draws a card for every job. In the real project the “database” becomes MongoDB, the “server” becomes Express (which saves you from writing the routing by hand), and the “browser” part becomes React components. Nothing else about the shape changes.
Why use the same language everywhere?

Using JavaScript on both sides has real, practical benefits for a learner. You learn one language instead of three. You can move code between the two sides, such as a function that checks an email address. The data you send, JSON, is already JavaScript's own format, so there is no translation step. And the huge package ecosystem, npm, serves both sides.

It is also fair to say what MERN is not. It is not the only good choice, and it is not always the best one: large teams often prefer TypeScript, a SQL database, or a framework such as Next.js. The ideas you learn here carry over to all of them: routes, middleware, schemas, tokens, state, effects and deployment are the same ideas with different names.

A word about versions. Libraries change. This course uses Node.js 20 or newer, Express 5, Mongoose 9, React 19 and Vite 7, and the zips pin those versions in `package.json`. If a command in a lesson fails on your machine, check the version first.
Your task

items: Download the solution zip for this lesson and unzip it.
Open a terminal in the unzipped folder and run `node examples/01-request-flow/trace.js`.
Change the `database` array: add a third job. Run the script again and check that a third card line appears.
Add a new route in the script: `GET /api/jobs/count` that answers `{ count: 3 }`, and call it with a second `fetch`. This is your first API route.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You see lines tagged `[browser]`, `[server]` and `[database]` in the order of the journey.
The browser line says `got status 200` and the right number of jobs.

content.text: Summary

items: React draws screens in the browser. Express on Node.js answers requests. MongoDB stores data.
The browser never talks to the database. It talks to your API.
Every feature is a request and a response with a status code, usually carrying JSON.

faqs.q: Do I need to know React or Node.js before this course?
faqs.a: No. You need basic JavaScript. The course teaches Node.js, Express, MongoDB and React from the start, and the next three lessons refresh the modern JavaScript you will use.

faqs.q: Is the MERN stack still worth learning?
faqs.a: Yes, as a way to learn how complete web applications work. The ideas (routes, middleware, schemas, tokens, components, state) apply to other stacks too. Which stack suits a job depends on the employer, so check the job adverts in your area.

faqs.q: Why does the browser not talk to MongoDB directly?
faqs.a: Anything in the browser can be read and changed by the visitor. Your API is the place where you check who is asking and whether the request is allowed and valid. Database passwords must never be in browser code.

lessons.title: Set Up Your Tools: Node.js, npm, Git, VS Code and MongoDB
lessons.description: Install and check everything you need for the MERN course on Windows, macOS or Linux, with a script that tells you what is missing.

content.text: A good setup saves hours later. This lesson lists exactly what to install, why, and how to check that it works. Nothing here is difficult, but small mistakes, such as an old version of Node.js, cause confusing errors later, so it is worth ten careful minutes now.
What you need

items: **Node.js 20 or newer** (the current LTS version is the safest choice). It runs your server and also the tools that build the React app. Download it from nodejs.org. It includes **npm**, the package manager.
**A code editor.** Visual Studio Code is free and works well, but any editor is fine. Useful extensions: ESLint, Prettier and REST Client (we use it in lesson 13).
**Git**, to save versions of your work and to deploy at the end. Install it from git-scm.com.
**A modern browser** with developer tools: Chrome, Edge or Firefox. Press F12 to open them. You will use the Network and Console tabs often.
**A MongoDB database** (lesson 14 shows both options: a free cloud database on Atlas, or MongoDB Community Edition on your computer). You do not need it yet.

content.text: Check your installation with a script
Instead of typing three commands and reading three outputs, run the small script from the lab. It asks your computer for the versions of Node.js, npm and Git, and tells you what to fix.

Notice what the script does: `process.versions.node` is information Node.js gives about itself, and `execSync('npm -v')` runs a command exactly as if you had typed it in the terminal. You will use both ideas again.
Using the terminal
You will type commands in a terminal for most of this course. On Windows use PowerShell or the terminal inside VS Code; on macOS and Linux use Terminal. The few commands you need on day one:

items: `cd folder-name` moves into a folder, and `cd ..` moves up one level.
`ls` (macOS and Linux) or `dir` (Windows) lists the files in the current folder.
`node file.js` runs a JavaScript file.
`npm install` downloads the packages listed in `package.json` into a `node_modules` folder.
Ctrl + C stops a running program. You will use this every day.

content.text: Never commit `node_modules/` or `.env` files to Git. The `.gitignore` file in the lab already lists them. Secrets that reach Git history are very hard to take back.
Folder habits that help

Keep the project in a folder whose path has no spaces or special characters, for example `C:\projects\mern-job-tracker` or `~/projects/mern-job-tracker`. Unzip each lesson's solution into a new folder rather than over your own work, so you can compare the two with your editor's “compare files” tool. When you are not sure why your code behaves differently from the lesson, comparing against the zip is the fastest way to find the one line that differs.
Your task

items: Install Node.js (LTS), Git and VS Code.
Unzip this lesson's solution and run `node examples/02-setup/check-setup.js`.
Fix every line that says `UPGRADE` or `MISSING`, then run it again until it says you are ready.
Run `git config --global user.name "Your Name"` and `git config --global user.email "you@example.com"` so your commits carry your name.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Each tool shows `OK` and the script ends with “You are ready for lesson 3.”
`node -v` prints v20 or higher.

content.text: Summary

items: You need Node.js 20+, an editor, Git and a browser. MongoDB comes in lesson 14.
The terminal runs your programs; Ctrl + C stops them.
Keep secrets and `node_modules` out of Git.

faqs.q: Which Node.js version should I install?
faqs.a: The current LTS (long term support) version, as long as it is version 20 or newer. LTS versions get fixes for longer and work with all the libraries in this course.

faqs.q: Can I use Windows for this course?
faqs.a: Yes. Everything works on Windows, macOS and Linux. Use PowerShell or the VS Code terminal on Windows. Commands that differ are noted in the lessons.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay for MongoDB?
faqs.a: No. MongoDB Community Edition is free to run on your own computer, and MongoDB Atlas has a free tier that is enough for this course. Check the Atlas site for the current limits.

lessons.title: Modern JavaScript You Need: let, const, Arrow Functions, Destructuring and Modules
lessons.description: The parts of modern JavaScript used in every MERN app, explained one by one, with a tour script you can run and change.

content.text: MERN code is written in the JavaScript of the last ten years, often called ES6 or ES2015+. If you learned JavaScript from older tutorials, some of the syntax will look new. Everything below appears again and again in the server and in React, so it is worth meeting it once, calmly, before the project starts.
Run the tour file after reading each section and change values to see what happens. Learning by changing working code is faster than only reading.
const and let, never var

`const` makes a variable that cannot be assigned again. `let` makes one that can. Use `const` by default and `let` only when the value must change, such as a counter. A `const` object can still be changed inside (you can add a property), but you cannot point the name at a different object. The old `var` has confusing scope rules, so modern code never uses it.
Template strings and objects

Back ticks create template strings, which can hold values: `` `Applied to ${company}` ``. Objects group related values, and **shorthand** lets you write `{ role }` instead of `{ role: role }` when the variable has the same name. You will write this constantly when building API responses.
Destructuring and spread

**Destructuring** pulls values out of objects and arrays into variables in one line: `const { role, salary: { max } } = job`. In React you will write `function JobCard({ job, onStatusChange })`, which is destructuring of the props object right in the parameter list.

**Spread** (`...`) copies the contents of an object or array into a new one. `{ ...job, status: 'interview' }` is a new object with all the old fields and a changed status, and the original is untouched. This matters a great deal: React state must be replaced, not edited in place, and spread is how you do it.
Arrow functions and array methods

An arrow function is a short function: `(j) => j.status === 'applied'`. Combined with the array methods `map`, `filter`, `find` and `reduce`, it replaces most `for` loops. `map` turns every item into something else (a list of jobs into a list of cards), `filter` keeps some items, `find` returns the first match, and `reduce` folds a list into one value, such as counts per status.
Optional chaining and defaults

`maybe.company?.name` returns `undefined` instead of crashing when `company` is missing. `??` gives a default only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`: `name ?? 'unknown'`. The older `||` replaces every falsy value, including `0` and an empty string, which is a common source of bugs, for example when a salary of 0 is replaced by a default.
Modules: import and export

Each file is a module. `export` makes something available to other files, and `import` brings it in. In Node.js, use `"type": "module"` in `package.json` (the server in this course does) and write the `.js` extension in relative imports: `import { formatSalary } from './helpers.js'`.
The tour
export const formatSalary = ({ min, max }) => `${min.toLocaleString('en-IN')} - ${max.toLocaleString('en-IN')}`;

Run it with `node examples/03-javascript/es6-tour.js`. Read the output next to the code. Pay attention to the line that prints `undefined interview`: it proves that spread made a copy, because the original `job` still has no status.
Your task

items: Run the tour and read each printed line against the code that produced it.
Use `filter` and `map` together to print only the roles of jobs whose status is `applied`.
Use `reduce` to total the `salary.max` of an array of three jobs.
Write a function `withStatus(job, status)` that returns a copy of the job with a new status and never changes the original. Check that the original is unchanged.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `node` runs the file with no errors.
Your `withStatus` returns a new object and the original job still has its old status.

content.text: Summary

items: `const` by default, `let` when needed, never `var`.
Destructuring takes values out; spread copies values in. Together they make non-mutating updates easy.
`map`, `filter`, `find` and `reduce` replace most loops.
Use `?.` and `??` for safe reads and honest defaults.

faqs.q: What is the difference between == and ===?
faqs.a: `===` compares value and type without converting, so `1 === "1"` is false. `==` converts first and gives surprising results. Use `===` everywhere.

faqs.q: Why does React need me to copy objects instead of changing them?
faqs.a: React decides whether to redraw by checking if state is a new value. If you edit an object in place, the reference is the same and React may not notice. Spread creates a new object, so React sees the change.

faqs.q: Do I need to learn classes and prototypes first?
faqs.a: Not for this course. Modern React uses function components, and the server code here uses plain functions and modules. Classes are useful to know later.

lessons.title: Asynchronous JavaScript: Callbacks, Promises, async/await and fetch
lessons.description: Why JavaScript does not wait, how promises and async/await work, how errors are caught, and how to run requests in parallel, with a script you can run.

content.text: Some things take time: reading a file, calling a database, asking another server for data. JavaScript has one main thread, so if it waited for each slow task, everything else, including the page or the server, would freeze. Instead it starts the task, carries on, and comes back when the result is ready. This is **asynchronous** programming, and every MERN app is full of it: each database query, each API call and each file upload is asynchronous.
Callbacks: the first idea

A **callback** is a function you give to something else to call later. `setTimeout(() => console.log('done'), 100)` means: run this function in 100 milliseconds. Callbacks work, but when one slow task depends on the result of another, you end up nesting them deeper and deeper, which is hard to read and hard to handle errors in.
Promises: a value that arrives later

A **promise** is an object that stands for a result that is not ready yet. It is in one of three states: pending, fulfilled (it has a value), or rejected (it has an error). You attach handlers with `.then()` for success and `.catch()` for errors, and you can chain them. Most libraries you will use, including `fetch` and Mongoose, return promises.
async and await: promises that read like normal code

Putting `async` in front of a function lets you use `await` inside it. `await` pauses that function (not the whole program) until the promise settles, then gives you the value. Errors become normal exceptions, so you catch them with `try / catch`. Compare the code in the file below: it does the same thing three ways.

Run it and read the output order carefully. The promise result prints before the callback, because the promise takes 50 ms and the callback 100 ms. Understanding that things finish in the order of their delays, not in the order you wrote them, is the key idea of this lesson.
Run tasks at the same time

If two things do not depend on each other, do not `await` them one after the other. `await Promise.all([a(), b()])` starts both at once and waits for both, so the total time is the slower of the two instead of the sum. You will use this pattern in lesson 18 to fetch a page of jobs and the total count in one go.
fetch: calling an API

`fetch(url)` is built into every modern browser and into Node.js 18 and newer. It returns a promise of a **Response**. Two details trip up almost every beginner. First, `fetch` only rejects when the network fails; a `404` or `500` answer is still a successful fetch, so you must check `response.ok` yourself. Second, reading the body is also asynchronous: `await response.json()`. The tour file shows the whole sequence.

The most common async bug: forgetting `await`. The code then holds a promise instead of the value, and prints `Promise { <pending> }` or silently skips the work. When a value looks strange, check that you awaited it.
Your task

items: Run the tour and note the order of the printed lines.
Change the delay in the callback to 10 ms and run it again. Which line moves, and why?
Write an `async` function `loadTwo()` that uses `Promise.all` to load two jobs, and time it with `console.time`. Then do it again with two separate awaits and compare the times.
Make `fetch` fail on purpose by calling a port nothing listens on, and catch the error with `try / catch`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: You can predict the order of the output before you run the file.
Your parallel version takes about as long as one request, not two.

content.text: Summary

items: Slow tasks do not block JavaScript. They finish later and hand back a result.
Promises represent that result; `async` and `await` make them readable.
`try / catch` handles errors; `Promise.all` runs independent tasks together.
`fetch` does not reject on 404 or 500; check `response.ok`.

faqs.q: Is async code the same as running things on several threads?
faqs.a: No. JavaScript runs your code on one thread. The waiting for files, networks and databases happens outside it, and your code continues when the result is ready.

faqs.q: When should I use Promise.all?
faqs.a: When tasks do not depend on each other, such as loading a list and a count. If one needs the result of the other, await them in order. Note that Promise.all rejects as soon as any one of them fails.

faqs.q: Why does fetch not throw an error for a 404?
faqs.a: Because from the network's point of view the request worked: the server answered. You decide what a 404 or 500 means in your app by checking response.ok or response.status.

lessons.title: HTTP, JSON and REST: Methods, Status Codes and Routes
lessons.description: How HTTP requests and responses are built, what the methods and status codes mean, how REST organises an API, and a REST server written with no libraries.

content.text: An API is a set of agreements: which addresses exist, what you can send to each, and what you get back. Almost all web APIs today follow the same conventions, called **REST**, which sit on top of **HTTP**. If you learn those conventions once, every API you meet will feel familiar, and your own API will be easy for others (and for your React app) to use.
An HTTP request

A request has a **method** that says what you want to do, a **path** that says which thing you mean, **headers** that carry extra information, and sometimes a **body** that carries data. A response has a **status code**, headers and sometimes a body. The two are always a pair: one request, one response.
The methods

items: `GET` reads data. It must never change anything. Browsers and caches rely on that.
`POST` creates something new, with the data in the body.
`PUT` replaces or changes something that exists. (`PATCH` is for partial changes; this course uses `PUT` for both to keep the API small.)
`DELETE` removes something.

content.text: Status codes you will use

items: **200 OK**: it worked. **201 Created**: a new thing was made. **204 No Content**: it worked and there is nothing to send back (usual for delete).

**400 Bad Request**: the data you sent is wrong. **401 Unauthorized**: we do not know who you are. **403 Forbidden**: we know you, but you may not do this. **404 Not Found**: no such thing. **409 Conflict**: it clashes with something that exists, such as an email already registered. **413 Payload Too Large**: a file or body is too big.
**500 Internal Server Error**: a bug on our side. The first digit is the family: 2 means success, 4 means the client made a mistake, 5 means the server did.

content.text: Choosing the right code is part of good API design. A React app can then react correctly: show field errors on 400, send the person to the login page on 401, and show “not found” on 404.
JSON

JSON is the text format for the body. It looks like a JavaScript object, but keys must be in double quotes and there are no functions or comments. `JSON.stringify(object)` makes text; `JSON.parse(text)` makes an object. Send the header `Content-Type: application/json` so the receiver knows how to read the body.
REST: nouns in the path, verbs in the method

REST names things, not actions. The path says *what* (`/api/jobs` or `/api/jobs/42`), and the method says *what to do with it*. So you do not make a path like `/api/getAllJobs` or `/api/deleteJob`; you use `GET /api/jobs` and `DELETE /api/jobs/42`. Collections are plural nouns, and one item is the collection plus an id. This is the shape of the API you will build.

This file is a complete REST server using only Node.js. Read it twice. Notice how much code goes into reading the body, matching the path with a regular expression and setting the status and headers. Express (lesson 9) removes almost all of that work, and the logic of each route stays the same. Seeing the long way once makes you appreciate, and understand, what the library does.
Your task

items: Run the server with `node examples/05-http-rest/rest-without-express.js`.
In a second terminal, run the four `curl` commands from the comment at the top, one by one. Use `-i` so you see the status line and headers.
Send a `POST` with an empty body and confirm you get `400` and a message.
Add a `PUT /api/jobs/:id` route that changes `company` and `role`, and returns `404` for an unknown id.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `GET` returns the list with status 200.
The `POST` returns 201 and the new job with an id.
Deleting twice returns 204 and then 404.

content.text: Summary

items: A request has a method, path, headers and maybe a body; a response has a status code and maybe a body.
Use `GET` to read, `POST` to create, `PUT` to change, `DELETE` to remove.
Status codes tell the client what happened: 2xx worked, 4xx your mistake, 5xx our bug.
REST: plural nouns in the path, the method says the action.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
faqs.a: 401 means the server does not know who you are (no or bad token). 403 means it knows you but you are not allowed to do that. In this course a job that belongs to someone else answers 404, so that we do not reveal that it exists.

faqs.q: Do I have to follow REST exactly?
faqs.a: No, it is a convention rather than a law. Following it makes your API predictable for other developers and tools, which is why we use it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
faqs.a: By the book, PUT replaces a whole item and PATCH changes only some fields. Many APIs, including the one in this course, use PUT for partial updates to keep things simple. What matters is that you document it and stay consistent.

lessons.title: Plan the Project: Features, API, Data Model and Folders
lessons.description: Plan a full stack app before coding: features, API routes, data model and folders. The Job Tracker plan you follow for the rest of the course.

content.text: Beginners often start with code and discover halfway that the pieces do not fit. Professionals spend a short time planning first, because changing a plan costs minutes and changing finished code costs days. The plan for a small app fits on one page. This lesson makes that page for the project you will build, and shows the thinking so you can repeat it for your own ideas.
Step 1: say what it does, in plain words

Write the purpose as two sentences a friend would understand. For us: *A signed-in person keeps a list of the jobs they applied for, moves each one through a status, adds notes and the resume they sent, and sees a few numbers about their search. Nobody can see anyone else's jobs.* Notice the last sentence. It is a **rule**, and rules like it drive the design: it is why every job must belong to a user, and why every query must filter by that user.
Step 2: list the screens

items: Sign in and Create account.
My jobs: numbers at the top, search and filters, a list with pages, and an “Add a job” form.
One job: edit the details, attach or replace the resume, delete.
A “not found” page.

content.text: Step 3: turn screens into API routes

For every thing a screen needs, write one route. A table is the clearest way. Look at the table in the plan file below: register, login, “who am I”, then the five job routes (list, add, read, change, delete), then statistics. Two details deserve attention. The list route takes **query parameters** for search, filter, sort and page, because the screen has those controls. And the statistics route is separate, because counting per status is a different question from listing jobs.

# Job Tracker: the plan

## What it does
A signed-in person keeps a list of the jobs they applied for, moves each one through a status
(saved, applied, interview, offer, rejected), adds notes, and sees a few numbers about their search.

## Folders
```
mern-job-tracker/
  package.json        shortcuts that run both apps
  docs/PLAN.md        this file
  server/             Node.js + Express + Mongoose  (the API)
  client/             React + Vite                  (the screens)
```

## API (JSON, all under /api)
| Method | Path              | What it does                         | Signed in? |
|--------|-------------------|--------------------------------------|------------|
| GET    | /api/health       | is the server up                     | no         |
| POST   | /api/auth/register| create an account                    | no         |
| POST   | /api/auth/login   | get a token                          | no         |
| GET    | /api/auth/me      | who am I                             | yes        |
| GET    | /api/jobs         | list my jobs (search, filter, page)  | yes        |
| POST   | /api/jobs         | add a job                            | yes        |
| GET    | /api/jobs/:id     | one job                              | yes        |
| PUT    | /api/jobs/:id     | change a job                         | yes        |
| DELETE | /api/jobs/:id     | remove a job                         | yes        |
| GET    | /api/jobs/stats   | counts per status                    | yes        |

## Data
- **User**: name, email (unique), passwordHash, createdAt
- **Job**: user (who owns it), company, role, location, status, salary note, notes, appliedOn, resumeFile

## Rules we keep
- A person can only ever see and change their own jobs.
- Passwords are never stored as text and never sent back.
- Secrets live in `.env`, never in Git.
Step 4: design the data

Next, list what you must remember about each thing. A **User** has a name, an email that must be unique, and a password (stored only as a hash, never as text). A **Job** has an owner, a company, a role, a place, a status from a fixed list, a free-text pay note, notes, and later an attached resume. Think about what to store as text and what as a fixed choice: the status has five allowed values, so we will make the database enforce them. Pay is free text on purpose, because people write it as “£28k”, “₦150,000 per month” or “₹600 a day”, and forcing a number and currency would lose information.
Step 5: choose the folders

Two apps in one repository keep everything together while keeping their tools apart. `server/` is the API with its own `package.json`. `client/` is the React app with its own. A small `package.json` at the top has shortcuts. The files below create that top-level shortcut file, so one command can install both apps and one command can start both.
`npm run setup` installs both apps. `npm run dev` uses the `concurrently` package to run the server and the client together in one terminal. You will use it from lesson 25, when the client appears.
Why plan the “boring” rules first?

Features are exciting, but **rules** are where real apps succeed or fail: who can see what, what happens with bad input, what is never stored. Writing three rules at the start (your own jobs only, no plain-text passwords, secrets in `.env`) means that you check every later lesson against them. Security added at the end is weaker than security designed at the start.
Your task

Draw the data model on paper: two boxes (User and Job) and an arrow from Job to User.

faqs.q: Is planning really needed for a small project?
faqs.a: A short plan is. Five minutes spent listing screens, routes and data prevents the most common problem: realising halfway that a field or a route is missing and having to change code in many places.

faqs.q: Why store the pay as text instead of a number?
faqs.a: Pay in adverts comes in many forms: per hour, per day, per month, in different currencies, sometimes as a range or “negotiable”. A text field keeps exactly what the advert said, and we do not guess or convert, which would risk showing wrong information.

faqs.q: Should the client and server be in one repository?
faqs.a: For a learning project and for small teams, yes: one place to clone, one history, easy to deploy together. Larger teams sometimes split them. The folders stay separate either way.

lessons.title: Node.js Basics: Modules, Files, Paths, Events and process
lessons.description: What Node.js adds to JavaScript: file access, paths, events and information about the running program, with an example you can run.

content.text: Node.js takes the JavaScript engine out of the browser and gives it abilities a browser deliberately does not have: reading and writing files, listening on network ports, and talking to the operating system. That makes it a good home for your back end. This lesson tours the few built-in parts you will meet in the rest of the course, so none of them feels strange later.
Built-in modules

Node.js comes with modules that you import by name with the `node:` prefix: `node:fs` (files), `node:path` (paths), `node:os` (information about the computer), `node:http` (network servers), `node:events` and `node:crypto`. The prefix tells readers and tools that this is a built-in, not a package from npm.
Files and paths

`fs/promises` gives you promise versions of the file functions, so you can `await` them: `readFile`, `writeFile`, `rm`, `mkdir`. Always build paths with `path.join(...)` instead of gluing strings with slashes, because Windows uses backslashes and macOS and Linux use forward slashes; `path.join` does the right thing on both. In ES modules there is no `__dirname`, so you create it from `import.meta.url` as the example does. You will do exactly this in lesson 36 when the server stores uploaded resumes.
Events

`EventEmitter` lets one part of a program announce that something happened (`emit`) and other parts react (`on`). It is the idea behind many Node.js objects: servers emit `request`, streams emit `data`, Mongoose connections emit `disconnected`. You will use `res.on('finish', ...)` in the request logger in lesson 10.
process: the running program

`process.env` holds **environment variables**: settings that come from outside your code, such as the port number or a database address. `process.argv` holds the command line words, `process.platform` the operating system, and `process.uptime()` how long the program has run. Environment variables are how you keep secrets and per-computer settings out of your source code, which is a rule you set in lesson 6.

Run it with `node examples/07-node/modules-and-files.js hello world`. You will see the extra words in `process.argv`. Now run it with a variable set: on macOS and Linux `PORT=8080 node examples/07-node/modules-and-files.js`, on Windows PowerShell `$env:PORT=8080; node examples/07-node/modules-and-files.js`. The printed port changes without any change to the code. That is the whole point of configuration by environment.
Node.js reads each file once and caches it. If you edit a file while the program runs, nothing changes until you restart. Starting in lesson 8 you will use `node --watch`, which restarts for you.
Your task

items: Run the example, then run it again with extra words and with `PORT` set.
Write a script `count-jobs.js` that reads a JSON file of jobs, prints how many there are for each status, and writes the result to `report.json`.
Make an `EventEmitter` that announces `job:added` and attach two listeners. Check that both run.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `process.env.PORT` shows your value when set and `(not set)` when not.
Your script writes a valid `report.json`.

content.text: Summary

items: Built-in modules (`node:fs`, `node:path`, `node:http`) give Node.js access to files, paths and the network.
Use `path.join` for paths; read settings from `process.env`.
Events let parts of a program react to each other.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Node.js and JavaScript in the browser?
faqs.a: The language is the same. Node.js adds file, network and operating system access, and has no page (no document or window). The browser has the page but, for safety, no direct file access.

faqs.q: Why use the node: prefix on imports?
faqs.a: It makes it clear that the import is a built-in module and cannot be confused with an npm package of the same name. It is optional but recommended.

faqs.q: What are environment variables?
faqs.a: Settings that live outside your code, in the shell or a .env file: ports, database addresses, secret keys. Your code reads them from process.env. This keeps secrets out of Git and lets the same code run in different places with different settings.

lessons.title: npm, package.json, Scripts and Environment Variables (dotenv)
lessons.description: Learn package.json, npm scripts, semantic versions and dotenv environment variables, and why .env stays out of Git.

content.text: Almost nobody writes a server from nothing. You use packages: small libraries other people wrote and published. **npm** is the tool that downloads them, and **package.json** is the file that lists what your project needs and how to run it. This lesson creates the `server` folder of the Job Tracker and sets up the two things every real project needs from day one: scripts to run it, and a safe way to keep settings out of the code.
package.json: the identity card of a project
`npm init -y` creates a `package.json`. The fields that matter are these.

items: **`"type": "module"`** switches the project to modern ES modules, so you write `import` and `export` instead of `require`. The whole course uses this.
**`scripts`** are named commands. `npm run dev` runs the `dev` script. `start` and `test` are special: you can write `npm start` and `npm test` without `run`.
**`dependencies`** are packages your program needs while it runs. **`devDependencies`** are only for development, such as test or build tools.

Version numbers like `^5.2.1` mean “5.2.1 or any newer 5.x version”. The exact versions that were installed are recorded in `package-lock.json`, which you **should** commit: it makes everyone, including your server, install the same versions.

content.text: Installing and the node_modules folder

`npm install express` downloads Express and its own dependencies into `node_modules/` and adds it to `dependencies`. `npm install` with no name installs everything listed in `package.json`, which is what you run after cloning a project. Never edit `node_modules`, never commit it (the `.gitignore` already excludes it), and delete it freely if something seems broken: `npm install` rebuilds it.

Install packages only from names you trust. A package with a similar-looking name to a famous one can be malicious. Check the spelling and the download count, and prefer well-known libraries, especially for security tasks such as hashing passwords.
Restarting automatically while you work

Node.js reads your code once, when it starts. To see a change you must stop and start again, which gets tiring. Since Node.js 18.11 there is a built-in fix: `node --watch index.js` restarts on every file change. That is our `dev` script, so you need no extra package such as nodemon.
Environment variables and .env

Passwords, database addresses and secret keys must not be written in code, because code goes into Git and Git history is permanent. They also differ from computer to computer: your laptop uses a local database and your server uses a hosted one. The solution is **environment variables**, read in code as `process.env.NAME`.

During development it is awkward to set variables in the terminal each time, so the `dotenv` package reads a file called `.env` and loads its lines into `process.env`. The top line of `index.js` below does it: `import 'dotenv/config'`. The `.env` file stays on your machine (it is in `.gitignore`). What you do commit is `.env.example`, a copy with the names but no secrets, so that a new developer knows what to fill in.

# Copy this file to .env and fill it in. Never commit .env to Git.
PORT=5000
Always read numbers with `Number(...)` and give a sensible default, as in `Number(process.env.PORT) || 5000`. Environment variables are always text, and a missing one is `undefined`.
Your task

items: Create `server/.env` by copying `.env.example` (do not commit it). Run `cd server && npm install && npm run dev`.
Change `PORT` in `.env`. Because `node --watch` watches your code files and not `.env`, stop the server with Ctrl + C and start it again to see the new value.
Run `npm run dev` with `NODE_ENV=production` set in your shell and read the second printed line.
Check that `git status` does not list `.env` (it should be ignored) but does list `.env.example`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The server prints the port from your `.env`.
`git status` never shows `.env` or `node_modules`.

content.text: Summary

items: `package.json` lists dependencies and scripts; commit `package-lock.json`.
`node --watch` restarts on changes, with no extra package.
Secrets and settings live in `.env`, never in Git; commit `.env.example` instead.

faqs.q: Should I commit package-lock.json?
faqs.a: Yes. It records the exact versions that were installed, so your teammates and your server install the same ones. Without it, a new install could pick a newer version and behave differently.

faqs.q: What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies?
faqs.a: dependencies are needed when the app runs in production. devDependencies, such as test runners and build tools, are only needed while developing. On a server you can install with --omit=dev to skip them.

faqs.q: Why is .env not committed to Git?
faqs.a: It holds secrets such as database passwords. Anything committed stays in Git history even after you delete it, and anyone with access to the repository could read it. Commit .env.example with empty values instead.

lessons.title: Your First Express Server: Routes, Parameters and Query Strings
lessons.description: Install Express 5, start a server, write routes for different methods, and read route parameters and query strings.

content.text: In lesson 5 you wrote a REST server by hand and saw how much work it was. **Express** is a small, very widely used library that does that plumbing for you: it matches the method and path, parses the URL, and gives you simple tools to send the answer. The server you build from this lesson is the same one that runs the finished Job Tracker.

This course uses **Express 5**, the current major version. If you find older tutorials for Express 4, nearly everything still applies. The most useful difference is that Express 5 automatically passes errors from `async` functions to your error handler, which removes a lot of try/catch code (you will see it in lesson 12).
The smallest server

Read it from the top. `express()` creates the **app**. `app.get(path, handler)` registers a route: when a `GET` request for that path arrives, Express calls the handler with two objects. `req` is the request: it holds the method, path, headers, parameters and body. `res` is the response: you call `res.json(...)` to send JSON, `res.status(201)` to set a status code, `res.sendFile(...)` to send a file. `app.listen(port, callback)` starts waiting for connections.
Route parameters and query strings
Two ways to send small pieces of information in the address itself are used constantly.

items: **Route parameters** are part of the path, marked with a colon: `/api/hello/:name`. A request for `/api/hello/Asha` gives `req.params.name === 'Asha'`. Use them to say *which* thing: `/api/jobs/64f...`.

**Query strings** come after a question mark: `/api/hello/Asha?shout=true`. Express puts them in `req.query`, so `req.query.shout === 'true'`. Use them for *options*: search text, filters, sorting and page numbers. Remember that all values arrive as text.

content.text: The rule of thumb: the path identifies a resource, and the query string adjusts how you view it. That is exactly how the Job Tracker's list route will work: `GET /api/jobs?status=applied&page=2`.
Order matters

Express checks routes in the order you wrote them and stops at the first match. If you put `/api/jobs/:id` before `/api/jobs/stats`, a request for `stats` is matched as an id. Put the specific routes first. You will meet this exact bug in lesson 19.
Try it in the browser and in the terminal

A `GET` route can be opened in the browser address bar: `http://localhost:5000/api/health`. For everything else use `curl` or a tool such as the REST Client (lesson 13). `curl -i http://localhost:5000/api/hello/Asha?shout=true` shows the whole response including the headers.
If you see “EADDRINUSE”, another program is already using that port, often an old copy of your own server. Stop it with Ctrl + C, or change `PORT` in `.env`.
Your task

items: Run `npm install` inside `server` (it now installs Express), then `npm run dev`.
Open `/api/health` in the browser. Reload and watch `time` change.
Call `/api/hello/Asha` and `/api/hello/Asha?shout=true`.
Add a route `GET /api/add/:a/:b` that returns the sum. Remember that parameters are text: convert with `Number()`, and answer `400` if either is not a number.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `/api/health` returns `{ "ok": true, "time": ... }`.
`shout=true` makes the message upper case.
Your add route answers 400 for `/api/add/x/2`.

content.text: Summary

items: `app.get(path, (req, res) => ...)` registers a route; `res.json()` answers.
Parameters (`req.params`) identify; query strings (`req.query`) adjust. Both arrive as text.
Routes are checked in order. Put specific paths before general ones.

faqs.q: What is the difference between req.params and req.query?
faqs.a: req.params holds values from the path itself (/jobs/:id). req.query holds values after the question mark (?page=2). Both are text, so convert numbers yourself.

faqs.q: Do I need Express, or can I use plain Node.js?
faqs.a: You can use plain Node.js, as lesson 5 showed, but you would write much more code for routing, parsing and errors. Express is small, popular and well documented, which is why most Node.js tutorials and jobs use it.

faqs.q: Why does my change not appear?
faqs.a: Node.js reads files once at start. Use npm run dev, which runs node --watch and restarts for you. If you edited .env, restart by hand because it is not watched.

lessons.title: Express Middleware: express.json, CORS and a Request Logger
lessons.description: How middleware works as a pipeline, why express.json and cors are needed, and how to write your own logger.

content.text: **Middleware** is the most important idea in Express. A middleware is a function that sits between the incoming request and your route. It can look at the request, change it, send an answer by itself, or pass it on by calling `next()`. Think of a security desk at an office: every visitor passes the desk first, and the desk may let them through, write down their name, or turn them away.

Everything else in this back end is built from middleware: reading JSON, allowing the React app to call the API, logging, signing in, rate limiting, uploads and error handling. Once you understand one, you understand all of them.
The shape of a middleware

It takes three arguments: `req`, `res` and `next`. It does its work and calls `next()`. If it forgot to call `next()` (and did not send an answer), the request would hang forever and the browser would spin. This logger uses an event from lesson 7: `res.on('finish', ...)` runs after the response has been sent, so it can report the final status code and the time taken.
Wiring the pipeline
`app.use(fn)` adds a middleware for every request. They run in the order you write them, then the matching route runs. Read the three in this file.

items: **The logger** runs first, so that every request is logged, even ones that later fail.

**`cors`** adds headers that tell the browser it is allowed to call this API from another address. A browser blocks a page at `localhost:5173` from reading answers from `localhost:5000` unless the server says that this origin is allowed. This is the browser's *same-origin policy*. Note that CORS only protects browsers: tools such as curl ignore it, so it is not a replacement for signing in.

**`express.json()`** reads the body of a request whose `Content-Type` is `application/json`, parses it, and puts the result in `req.body`. Without it `req.body` is `undefined`. The `limit` of 100 kb rejects absurdly large bodies, which protects the server from being flooded.

content.text: Try the pipeline

The route at the bottom of the file, `POST /api/echo`, shows that `req.body` works. Send it a body with curl: `curl -i -X POST localhost:5000/api/echo -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"hello":"world"}'`. Then remove the `Content-Type` header and see that `youSent` becomes empty: Express only parses JSON when it is told the body is JSON.
Middleware for one route

A middleware can also be placed in front of a single route: `app.get('/private', checkSomething, handler)`. You will use that for signing in (lesson 22), for rate limiting the login route (lesson 23) and for file uploads (lesson 36). Global middleware is for things every request needs; route middleware is for things only some routes need.

Order is a common source of bugs. `express.json()` must come *before* the routes that read `req.body`. The error handler (lesson 12) must come *after* the routes. When something does not work, print the order of your `app.use` lines.
Your task

items: Run the server and call `/api/health`. Look at the logger line in the terminal.
Send the echo request with and without the `Content-Type` header. Compare `req.body`.

Write a new middleware `addRequestId` that creates a random id with `crypto.randomUUID()`, stores it on `req.id`, and sets an `X-Request-Id` response header. Add it before the logger and include the id in the log line.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Each request prints one line with the method, path, status and time.
The echo route returns what you sent only when the JSON header is present.
Your responses have an `X-Request-Id` header.

content.text: Summary

items: Middleware is a function `(req, res, next)`: handle the request or call `next()`.
Order matters: they run top to bottom, so put `express.json()` before the routes.
CORS tells browsers which sites may call the API. It is not security by itself.

faqs.q: Why does my request hang forever?
faqs.a: A middleware or route neither sent a response nor called next(). Every path through your code must end in a response or a call to next.

faqs.q: What is CORS and why do I get a CORS error?
faqs.a: Browsers refuse to let a page read answers from another origin (different address or port) unless the server allows it with CORS headers. In this course the server allows the React address, and in production both are served from one origin so no CORS is needed.

faqs.q: Does CORS protect my API from attackers?
faqs.a: No. CORS is enforced by browsers only. Anyone can call your API with curl or a script. Protection comes from signing in, authorization checks, validation and rate limiting.

lessons.title: Routers and Controllers: A Clean Express Project Structure
lessons.description: Split an Express app into routers and controllers so that it stays readable as it grows, using an in-memory jobs API.

content.text: One file with every route works for a demo, but a real API has dozens of routes, and a 600-line `index.js` is hard to read, test and change. The standard answer is to split by responsibility. A **router** lists the paths of one feature and says which function handles each. A **controller** holds the functions that do the work. The main file only assembles them.

In this lesson you build the whole jobs API, with five routes (list, read, create, change, delete), storing jobs in an array in memory. That is not a real database, since everything vanishes when the server restarts, but it lets us focus on structure and replace the storage in lesson 17 without touching the routes.
The router

`Router()` creates a mini app that can have routes and middleware of its own. Reading this file tells you the whole API of the feature at a glance: five lines, each with a method, a path and a handler. Notice that the paths here are relative: `'/'` and `'/:id'`. The main file decides the prefix.
The controller

Each exported function is one route handler. They are plain functions of `(req, res)`, so they are easy to read and, later, to test. For now they work on the `jobs` array. Look at how `getJob`, `updateJob` and `deleteJob` all start by finding the job and answering `404` when it does not exist. Repeating that pattern is a hint that it can be extracted into a helper, and in lesson 12 it will be.
Mounting it

`app.use('/api/jobs', jobsRouter)` says: any request whose path starts with `/api/jobs` goes to this router, with that prefix removed. So `GET /api/jobs/5` reaches `router.get('/:id')`. When you add users, files or statistics you add one line here and one new pair of files, and the rest of the app is untouched.
A rule of thumb for what goes where

items: **Routes**: paths, methods and which middleware runs. No logic.
**Controllers**: read the request, call the data layer, choose the status code and the answer.
**Models** (from lesson 16): how data looks and how it is stored.
**Middleware** and **utils**: things reused by many routes.

content.text: This is a convention, not magic. Smaller apps sometimes merge two layers, and larger ones add a “service” layer between controllers and models. What matters is that you can say, for any piece of code, which layer it belongs to and find it fast.

Right now a request with a missing `company` creates a broken job, and an `id` like `abc` is treated as a number. Do not worry: lesson 12 adds validation and error handling. It is more instructive to see the problem first.
Your task

items: Run the server and call `GET /api/jobs`, `GET /api/jobs/1`, and `GET /api/jobs/99`.
Create a job with `POST` and a JSON body, then change its status with `PUT`, then delete it.
Send a `POST` with an empty body `{}`. What was stored? Write down what you would want to happen instead.
Add a third route file `routes/health.js` with its own router and mount it at `/api/health`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: All five routes answer with the right status codes (200, 201, 204, 404).
An empty `POST` is accepted. You have seen the problem that lesson 12 fixes.

content.text: Summary

items: Routers list paths; controllers do the work; `index.js` assembles them.
`app.use('/api/jobs', router)` mounts a router under a prefix.
Keeping layers separate lets you change storage later without touching routes.

faqs.q: Do I have to use a controllers folder?
faqs.a: No, it is a convention. Small apps can keep handlers next to routes. The benefit of separating them is that the route file reads like a table of contents and the handlers are easy to find and test.

faqs.q: What does mounting a router do to the path?
faqs.a: app.use("/api/jobs", router) removes the prefix before the router sees the path. So a request for /api/jobs/5 matches router.get("/:id") with id 5.

faqs.q: Why store data in an array first?
faqs.a: It lets you learn routing and structure without a database. Because the routes and controller functions keep the same names, switching to MongoDB in lesson 17 changes only the bodies of the controller functions.

steps.say: As the API grows, one big file becomes hard to read. We split it by responsibility.
index.js only mounts routers: /api/jobs goes to the jobs router.
A router lists the URLs and the functions that answer them, and nothing else.
Controllers hold the logic: read the input, do the work, send the reply.
Controllers talk to the data layer. When we move to MongoDB, only this part changes.

lessons.title: Validation and Error Handling in Express: HttpError and an Error Middleware
lessons.description: Never trust the client: check input, return helpful 400 answers with field errors, and send every failure through one error handler.

content.text: The most important sentence in back end development is: **never trust the client**. Anyone can send anything to your API: missing fields, numbers where text is expected, a ten-megabyte string, JSON that is not JSON. If your code assumes good input, the first bad request either crashes the server or, worse, stores garbage. This lesson adds two protections to the jobs API: **validation** (check and clean the input) and **error handling** (turn every failure into a clear, safe answer).
Validation: check, clean, then use

`cleanJob` receives the body and does three things. It **checks** that required fields exist and have a sensible length. It **cleans** the values with `trim()`. And it **copies only the fields it knows**, so that if a client adds `{ "admin": true }`, that field is simply ignored. This last step prevents a class of bugs called *mass assignment*. Problems are collected in one object so the client can show all of them at once, not one per attempt.

The `partial` option exists for updates: when changing a job, every field is optional, but the ones you send must still be valid. That is why the function checks `body[field] === undefined && partial` first.
A custom error that carries a status

A normal `Error` has a message but no idea about HTTP. `HttpError` adds a `status` and optional `details`. Now any code, a controller, a validator or a middleware, can `throw new HttpError(404, 'Job not found')` and know the right answer will be sent. Throwing is better than writing `res.status(404).json(...)` and `return` in every place, because it stops the function immediately and keeps the happy path clean.
One place that answers every error

An **error-handling middleware** has *four* parameters, `(err, req, res, next)`. That is how Express recognises it, so keep all four even if `next` is unused. Express sends any thrown or passed error to it. It also receives errors from `async` functions in Express 5, so a rejected `await` ends up here without a `try/catch`.

items: Known errors (those with a `status` below 500) are shown to the client with their message and details.

Unknown errors are bugs. They are **logged** on the server, but the client only gets a generic “Something went wrong”. Showing the real message could leak file paths or database details to an attacker.
`notFound` handles requests that matched no route and gives a JSON 404 instead of Express's default HTML page.

content.text: Using it in the controller

Compare this controller with lesson 11. The repeated `if (!job) return res.status(404)...` is now one small `find` function that throws. The create and update routes call `cleanJob`, so bad input never reaches the data. And `index.js` registers `notFound` after all the routes and `errorHandler` last of all, because Express treats the error middleware as the final stop.
Never put error details such as stack traces in the response in production. They help attackers. Log them on the server instead, where only you can read them.
Your task

items: Run the server. Send `POST /api/jobs` with `{ "company": "", "status": "maybe" }` and read the `details` object in the answer.
Send invalid JSON (for example `{ "company": `) and confirm you get `400` with a clear message, not an HTML page.
Call `GET /api/nothing` and `GET /api/jobs/999`. Both should answer 404 in JSON.
Add a `location` field to `cleanJob` (optional, at most 120 characters).

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Bad input answers 400 and tells you which fields are wrong.
Unknown routes and missing jobs answer 404 as JSON.
A deliberate bug (throw a normal Error in a route) answers 500 with a generic message and logs the details in your terminal.

content.text: Summary

items: Check, clean and whitelist input; return all field errors together.
Throw `HttpError` anywhere; one error middleware (four parameters, registered last) sends the answer.
Log unknown errors on the server; never show their details to the client.

faqs.q: Why does the error middleware need four parameters?
faqs.a: Express decides that a function is an error handler by counting its parameters. With four (err, req, res, next) it is used for errors. With three it is a normal middleware, even if you meant it as an error handler.

faqs.q: Should validation be on the server or the client?
faqs.a: Both, for different reasons. Client validation gives quick, friendly feedback. Server validation is the one that protects you, because the client can be bypassed. Never rely only on the client.

faqs.q: Do I need a validation library?
faqs.a: Not for a small API like this. Libraries such as Zod or Joi help when you have many shapes of data, and the ideas are the same: describe the rules, check, and return clear errors. Doing it by hand once helps you understand what they do.

Validation checks the input and keeps only the fields we allow.
On a problem we throw an HttpError with a status such as 400 and a clear message.

lessons.title: Test Your API: REST Client, Postman, curl and a Smoke Script
lessons.description: Ways to try an API without a front end, from one-off requests to a script that checks a whole flow and prints PASS or FAIL.

content.text: You now have a working API but no screen. How do you know it works? You call it. This lesson shows the three levels of testing an API by hand and by script, and gives you a **smoke script** you will keep using, extended, until the end of the course.
Level 1: one request at a time
There are three common tools, and they all do the same job: build a request and show the response.

items: **curl** is in every terminal. `curl -i -X POST localhost:5000/api/jobs -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"company":"Acme","role":"Clerk"}'` sends a POST and shows the status line and headers because of `-i`. It is best for quick checks and for scripts on a server.
**Postman** and similar apps (Insomnia, Thunder Client) give you a window with saved requests. Good for exploring someone else's API.

**The REST Client extension for VS Code** reads a plain `.http` file where each request is a few lines separated by `###`, and you click “Send Request”. The file is text, so you can commit it, and your whole team shares the same examples. We use it here.

content.text:
### Open this file in VS Code with the "REST Client" extension and click "Send Request" above a line.
### Or copy each one into Postman / Thunder Client / curl.

@base = http://localhost:5000/api

### Is the server up?
GET {{base}}/health

### List jobs
GET {{base}}/jobs

### Add a job
POST {{base}}/jobs
Content-Type: application/json

{ "company": "Acme Logistics", "role": "Dispatcher", "status": "applied" }

### Add a job with a mistake (expect 400 and a details object)
POST {{base}}/jobs
Content-Type: application/json

{ "company": "", "status": "maybe" }

### One job
GET {{base}}/jobs/1

### Change a job
PUT {{base}}/jobs/1
Content-Type: application/json

{ "status": "interview" }

### Delete a job
DELETE {{base}}/jobs/1

### A job that does not exist (expect 404)
GET {{base}}/jobs/999

Open this file in VS Code with the REST Client extension installed. The line `@base = http://localhost:5000/api` defines a variable used as `{{base}}` in every request. Run them in order and watch the answers. Pay special attention to the one with a deliberate mistake, which should answer `400` with a `details` object, and to the one for a job that does not exist, which should answer `404`.
Level 2: a script that checks the answers

Clicking is fine for exploring, but you want a quick way to know that nothing has broken after a change. A **smoke test** runs the main paths through the real running server and reports PASS or FAIL. It is called a smoke test from electronics: switch it on and see whether smoke comes out. It does not prove the app is perfect; it quickly catches the obvious breakage.

Read the two small helpers at the top. `check(name, ok)` prints a line and counts failures. `call(method, path, body)` wraps `fetch`, turns the body into JSON, and returns `{ status, data }`, so every test line is short. At the end, `process.exit(1)` when any check failed gives the script a non-zero exit code, which is what automated systems use to know that something broke. In lesson 22 the script learns to sign in, and in lesson 24 you will meet real automated tests.
Level 3: automated tests

A smoke script needs a running server and checks the main flow. A real **automated test suite** starts its own copy of the app, uses its own database, runs dozens of small checks and runs on every change. You will build one in lesson 24. The tests will be easier to write because of how you structured the code today.
Test the unhappy paths as carefully as the happy ones. Most real bugs and most attacks live in what happens with missing, wrong or hostile input, not in what happens when everything is perfect.
Your task

items: Start the server with `npm run dev`, then in a second terminal run `npm run smoke`.
Break something on purpose: change the `404` in `getJob` to `500`, save, and run the smoke script. Which line fails?
Add two checks to the script: `PUT` with an invalid status answers `400`, and `GET /api/jobs/abc` answers `404`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Every line starts with PASS and the script ends with “All checks passed”.
The deliberate break produces a FAIL line with the answer that came back.

content.text: Summary

items: Use curl or a `.http` file for single requests.
A smoke script runs the main flow and exits with a non-zero code on failure.
Test bad input as carefully as good input.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a smoke test and unit tests?
faqs.a: A smoke test calls a running app over HTTP and checks the main flow quickly. Unit and integration tests run small pieces or a whole app in isolation, usually with their own database, and cover many more cases. You need both over time.

faqs.q: Can I test the API without writing code?
faqs.a: Yes. curl, Postman or the REST Client extension send single requests with no code. Writing a script is what lets you repeat the same checks after every change.

faqs.q: Why does the script call process.exit(1) on failure?
faqs.a: A non-zero exit code is how programs tell their caller that something failed. Build servers and scripts check it, so a failing smoke test can stop a deployment.

lessons.title: What Is MongoDB? Documents, Collections, Atlas and mongosh
lessons.description: How MongoDB stores documents in collections, how it differs from SQL, how to get a free Atlas database, and the mongosh commands to try.

content.text: Until now the Job Tracker has kept its data in an array, which disappears when the server stops. A **database** keeps data safely on disk and lets many requests read and change it at once, quickly and without corrupting it. **MongoDB** is a *document database*. Instead of rows in tables, it stores **documents**, which look almost exactly like the JavaScript objects you already use, which is one of the reasons it fits so naturally into a JavaScript stack.
Documents, collections and databases

items: A **document** is one record: `{ company: 'Acme', role: 'Dispatcher', status: 'applied', tags: ['night shift'] }`. It can hold nested objects and arrays. It is stored in a format called BSON (binary JSON) that adds types such as dates and ids.
A **collection** is a group of documents, similar to a table. Our app will have a `users` collection and a `jobs` collection.
A **database** holds collections. Our app uses one called `job_tracker`.
Every document has an **`_id`**, a unique value that MongoDB creates for you if you do not (an `ObjectId`, which is displayed as 24 hexadecimal characters).

content.text: How is that different from SQL?

In a SQL database every row in a table has the same columns, set in advance, and you spread related data across tables and join them when reading. In MongoDB documents in the same collection may have different fields, and you often keep related data together inside one document. That flexibility is useful when the shape of data changes, but it is also a trap: without rules, a collection can fill up with inconsistent documents. That is why in lesson 16 we add a **schema** with Mongoose. Neither model is better in every case. SQL databases are excellent when data has many relationships, strict rules and reports across tables; document databases are comfortable when you read and write whole objects, as most web apps do.
Get a database: two options

# Lesson 14: set up MongoDB

Pick one:

**A. MongoDB Atlas (free cloud database, nothing to install)**
1. Create an account at mongodb.com/atlas and make a free (M0) cluster.
2. Database Access: add a user with a password. Network Access: allow your current IP address.
3. Connect > Drivers: copy the connection string. It looks like `mongodb+srv://USER:PASSWORD@cluster0.xxxxx.mongodb.net/job_tracker`.

**B. MongoDB Community Edition on your computer**
1. Install it from mongodb.com/try/download/community and start the service.
2. Your connection string is `mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/job_tracker`.

Then try the shell script: `mongosh "<connection string>" examples/14-mongodb/queries.mongosh.js`.

**MongoDB Atlas** is the hosted service by the makers of MongoDB, and its free tier is enough for this course. You do not install anything, and later the same cluster can serve your deployed app. Two settings catch beginners out: the **Network Access** list must include your current IP address (or, for learning only, you may allow all addresses, but never do that for real data), and the **database user** is separate from your Atlas login. **Community Edition** runs on your own computer and works offline; it is free too.

Your connection string contains a password. Treat it like one: it goes in `.env`, never in code, never in Git, never in a screenshot. If it leaks, change the database user's password in Atlas at once.
Try the shell

`mongosh` is MongoDB's command line. The script below inserts three jobs, searches them in several ways, changes one, groups and counts them, deletes one and drops its demo database. Read each part, because the operations are the same ones Mongoose will perform for you.

items: **`insertMany`** adds documents; the collection is created on first write.

**`find(filter, projection)`** returns matching documents. Filters can use operators that start with `$`: `$in`, `$gte`, `$or`. A dotted path such as `'salary.min'` reaches inside a nested object, and `tags: 'bank'` matches an array that *contains* `'bank'`.
**`updateOne(filter, update)`** needs an update operator like `$set` or `$push`; without one MongoDB would replace the whole document.
**`aggregate`** runs a pipeline of stages. `$group` with `$sum: 1` counts documents per value. You will build the Job Tracker's statistics screen with exactly this in lesson 19.

content.text: Your task

items: Create an Atlas free cluster (or install Community Edition) and copy the connection string.
Install `mongosh` and run the script against your database: `mongosh "<connection string>" examples/14-mongodb/queries.mongosh.js`.
Edit the script: add a `location` to each job and find only the jobs in one place.

items: The script prints the filtered jobs, the grouped counts and “left: 2”.
You can connect with `mongosh` and list databases with `show dbs`.

content.text: Summary

items: MongoDB stores JSON-like documents in collections; every document has an `_id`.
Use Atlas (hosted) or Community Edition (local). Keep the connection string secret.
Filters, `$set`/`$push` updates and aggregation pipelines are the core operations.

faqs.q: Is MongoDB better than SQL?
faqs.a: Neither is better in every case. MongoDB suits data you read and write as whole objects and whose shape changes. SQL databases suit strongly related data, strict rules and cross-table reports. Many real systems use both.

faqs.q: Is the free Atlas tier enough for learning?
faqs.a: Yes, for a course project. Limits and features change over time, so check the Atlas pricing page for the current free tier. Do not store real personal data on a free learning cluster.

faqs.q: What is an ObjectId?
faqs.a: It is MongoDB's default _id type: 12 bytes shown as 24 hex characters. It is unique and roughly increases over time because it begins with a timestamp. Mongoose gives it to you for every new document.

lessons.title: Connect Express to MongoDB with Mongoose
lessons.description: Install Mongoose, connect with a connection string from .env, start the server only after the database is ready, and show the database state in a health.

content.text: Your server can now talk HTTP. Next it must talk to MongoDB. You could use the official driver, which sends raw commands, but most MERN projects use **Mongoose**, a library on top of the driver. Mongoose adds three things you will want: **schemas** (rules for what a document must look like), **models** (objects that have methods like `find` and `create`), and helpful validation and error messages. This lesson only makes the connection. The next three use it.
The connection string

# Copy this file to .env and fill it in. Never commit .env to Git.
PORT=5000
CLIENT_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
# Atlas: mongodb+srv://USER:PASSWORD@cluster0.xxxxx.mongodb.net/job_tracker
# Local: mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/job_tracker
MONGODB_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/job_tracker

A connection string is an address plus credentials plus the database name. Atlas gives you one starting with `mongodb+srv://`. A local one looks like `mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/job_tracker`. The last part, after the final slash, is the **database name**; if it does not exist MongoDB creates it on first write. Put the real value in `server/.env`, and restart the server, because `.env` is not watched.
Connecting

`mongoose.connect(uri, options)` returns a promise. We wrap it in a function so the main file stays short and so tests (lesson 24) can pass a different address. The option `serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 8000` is a kindness to yourself: without it, a wrong address or a blocked IP makes the program hang for about 30 seconds before failing. With it you see the real error in 8 seconds. The `disconnected` listener logs when the connection drops, for example when your Wi-Fi does.
Start listening only when the database is ready

The server used to start with `app.listen` straight away. Now it first awaits `connectDB()` and only then listens, inside a `try/catch`. If the database is not available, the program prints a clear message and exits with `process.exit(1)`, instead of accepting requests it cannot serve. This **fail fast** habit is much better than a server that is “up” but returns errors on every call. (Top-level `await` works here because the project uses ES modules.)

The health route now reports `mongoose.connection.readyState`. The value `1` means connected; `0` disconnected, `2` connecting, `3` disconnecting. Monitoring tools can call this route to know that the whole app, not only the web server, is healthy. In lesson 37 it will answer `503` when the database is down.
Common connection problems

items: **“bad auth” or “Authentication failed”**: the user name or password is wrong, or the password contains special characters that must be URL-encoded (`@` becomes `%40`).
**Timeout or “ECONNREFUSED”**: for Atlas, your IP is not in Network Access; for local MongoDB, the service is not running.
**It connects but you see no data in Atlas**: you are looking at a different database name than the one in the string.

content.text: Your task

items: Run `npm install` in `server` (it adds Mongoose) and put your connection string in `server/.env` as `MONGODB_URI`.
Start the server and call `/api/health`. You should see `db: connected`.
Break the string on purpose (wrong password). How long does it take to fail, and what does it print?
Stop your local MongoDB (or remove your IP from Atlas) while the server runs and watch the log.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The terminal prints “MongoDB connected: job_tracker”.
`/api/health` answers `db: connected`.
A wrong string makes the program exit within about 8 seconds with a clear message.

content.text: Summary

items: Mongoose adds schemas, models and validation on top of the MongoDB driver.
The connection string lives in `.env`; the part after the last slash is the database name.
Connect first, listen second, and exit with a clear message if the database is down.

faqs.q: Do I need Mongoose, or can I use the MongoDB driver directly?
faqs.a: You can use the driver directly. Mongoose adds schemas, validation, defaults and convenient model methods, which suits most web apps and keeps data consistent. Some teams prefer the plain driver for more control.

faqs.q: Why does my password with an @ sign fail?
faqs.a: In a connection string the @ separates the credentials from the host, so one inside the password confuses the parser. URL-encode special characters (@ becomes %40) or choose a password without them.

faqs.q: Why wait for the database before calling listen?
faqs.a: A server that accepts requests but has no database fails every call in confusing ways. Failing at start with a clear message is easier to notice and fix, and process managers such as pm2 can restart it.
