lessons.title: Mongoose Schemas and Models: Types, Validation, Defaults and Timestamps
lessons.description: Describe what a Job looks like, add validation rules and defaults, hide internal fields in JSON output, and test the model without a server.

content.text: A MongoDB collection will happily store anything. If one document has `company` and another has `Company` and a third has `company: 42`, MongoDB does not complain, and your React app will break in strange ways. A Mongoose **schema** is the rulebook that prevents this. A **model** is built from the schema and is the object you use to create, read, update and delete documents.
The Job schema
Walk through it field by field.

items: **`type`** converts values to that type when possible and rejects them when not. `String`, `Number`, `Date`, `Boolean`, `ObjectId` and arrays are the ones you will use.
**`required: [true, 'message']`** fails validation when the field is missing or empty. The second item is the error message the client will see.

**`trim: true`** removes spaces at both ends before saving, so `'  Acme '` is stored as `'Acme'`. Other helpful string options are `lowercase`, `minlength`, `maxlength` and `match` (a regular expression).
**`enum`** lists the allowed values. Our `status` can only be one of five words. Anything else is rejected before it reaches the database.
**`default`** fills a value when none is given. A new job starts as `saved`.

content.text: `salaryNote` is a string on purpose. As lesson 6 explained, advertised pay is written in many ways and converting it would lose information or show wrong numbers.
Timestamps and the toJSON transform
`{ timestamps: true }` makes Mongoose maintain `createdAt` and `updatedAt` for you. You will sort by `createdAt` in lesson 18, and the React app uses `updatedAt` in lesson 31.

The `toJSON` setting controls what `res.json(job)` sends. `virtuals: true` adds `id`, a text version of `_id`, which is friendlier to React. The transform then deletes `_id` and `__v` (a version counter used internally). Shaping output in one place means no route can forget to hide something. In lesson 20 the same trick will hide password hashes, which is the reason it is worth learning now.

A schema only applies to writes that go through Mongoose. Anyone who connects to the database directly (with mongosh or Compass) can still write anything. Keep database credentials private and give application users only the permissions they need.
Using the model without a server

You do not need Express to try a model. `new Job({...})` builds a document in memory, `validateSync()` checks the rules and returns the problems without touching the database, and `toJSON()` shows what would be sent. The script below does exactly that.

Run it with `node scripts/model-demo.js` from the `server` folder. You will see two validation messages (company and role are required, status is not allowed) and then a good job with its trimmed company and the default status. This is the same check that will run automatically every time a route creates or updates a job.
Your task

items: Create `server/models/Job.js` from the lesson and run `node scripts/model-demo.js`.
Add a `url` field (string, optional, must start with `http://` or `https://` using `match`). Test it with a good and a bad value in the demo script.
Add a `source` field with `enum: ['website', 'referral', 'agency', 'other']` and a default of `other`.
Make `appliedOn` default to nothing, and write down why a default of `Date.now` would be wrong for a job with status `saved`.

The good job is trimmed and has `status: 'saved'` and an `id`.

content.text: Summary

items: A schema defines types, rules and defaults; a model is what you query with.
Validation messages from the schema become the field errors the client shows.
`toJSON` decides what leaves the server, so hide internals there.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a schema and a model?
faqs.a: The schema describes the shape and rules of a document. The model is created from a schema with mongoose.model() and gives you the methods to work with a collection: create, find, update, delete.

faqs.q: Does MongoDB itself enforce my schema?
faqs.a: No. The schema is enforced by Mongoose in your application code. MongoDB also has its own optional validation rules, but Mongoose validation is the usual first line of defence. Anything written outside Mongoose is not checked by it.

faqs.q: What does timestamps: true do?
faqs.a: It adds createdAt and updatedAt fields and keeps them up to date automatically, so you can sort by newest and know when something last changed.

lessons.title: CRUD with Mongoose: Create, Read, Update and Delete in Express
lessons.description: Replace the in-memory array with MongoDB: create, find, update and delete with Mongoose, validate ids and return friendly errors.

content.text: This is the lesson where the Job Tracker becomes real. The routes and the router stay exactly as they were. Only the body of each controller function changes, from “work on an array” to “work on MongoDB”. That is the payoff of the structure from lesson 11.
The four operations

items: **Create**: `Job.create(data)` builds a document, runs validation and saves it. It returns the saved document, including its new `_id`.
**Read**: `Job.find(filter)` returns an array; `Job.findById(id)` returns one document or `null`. Chain `.sort({ createdAt: -1 })` to order newest first.

**Update**: `Job.findByIdAndUpdate(id, changes, options)`. The option `new: true` returns the document *after* the change (the default returns the old one). `runValidators: true` is essential: **update operations skip the schema rules unless you ask for them**, which would let `{ status: 'maybe' }` slip in.
**Delete**: `Job.findByIdAndDelete(id)` removes it and returns the removed document, or `null`.

content.text: Every one of these is asynchronous, so every one needs `await`. Because the controller functions are `async` and Express 5 forwards rejected promises to the error handler, you do not need `try/catch` in each one. A validation failure inside `create` simply throws, and the error middleware answers.
Do not trust the body: pick the fields

`pickJobFields` copies only the fields we allow. Passing `req.body` straight to `Job.create` is a classic security hole: a client could add fields you never meant to be settable. A whitelist makes the allowed fields explicit. (In lesson 22 the owner field is added by the server from the signed-in user and never read from the body, which is the most important use of this habit.)

`checkId` is a **param middleware**: `router.param('id', checkId)` runs for every route that has `:id` in the path. A text that is not a valid ObjectId would otherwise make Mongoose throw a `CastError`. Here it answers `404` straight away, which also avoids confirming anything about how ids look.
Translating database errors

`translate` recognises the errors that Mongoose and MongoDB throw and turns them into friendly answers. A `ValidationError` becomes `400` with one message per field, in the same shape as lesson 12, so a React form can show them. A `CastError` becomes `400`. A MongoDB duplicate-key error (code `11000`, which you will meet for emails in lesson 20) becomes `409 Conflict`. Anything else stays a generic `500` and is logged.
`findByIdAndUpdate` with `new: true` and `runValidators: true` is the pair to remember. Forgetting `runValidators` is one of the most common ways invalid data gets into a Mongoose app.
Your task

Open your database in Atlas (or Compass) and find the `jobs` collection that was created by the first `POST`.
Restart the server and call `GET /api/jobs`. The data is still there. That is persistence.
Try to update a job with `{ "status": "maybe" }`. Then remove `runValidators: true` from the update and try again. What changed?

An invalid status on update answers 400 with a message for `status`.

items: `create`, `find`, `findById`, `findByIdAndUpdate`, `findByIdAndDelete` cover CRUD.
Updates need `{ new: true, runValidators: true }`.
Whitelist body fields; validate ids; translate database errors into 400, 404 and 409.

faqs.q: Why does my update accept invalid data?
faqs.a: Update methods such as findByIdAndUpdate do not run schema validators unless you pass runValidators: true. Add it to every update, and also use new: true to receive the changed document.

faqs.q: What is a CastError?
faqs.a: Mongoose throws it when it cannot convert a value to the schema type, most often a text that is not a valid ObjectId in a /:id route. Validate the id first and answer 404 or 400.

faqs.q: Should I use try/catch in every controller?
faqs.a: Not with Express 5. It passes errors thrown or rejected inside async handlers to your error middleware automatically. Use try/catch only when you need to clean up or handle a specific error locally.

lessons.title: Search, Filter, Sort and Paginate with Mongoose, and Why Indexes Matter
lessons.description: Build a list endpoint with text search, status filter, sorting and pages, protect it from abuse, and add indexes so it stays fast.

content.text: A list of ten jobs is easy. A list of ten thousand cannot be sent in one answer, and a person cannot read it anyway. Real list endpoints let the client say **which** items (filter and search), **in what order** (sort) and **how many at a time** (pagination). This lesson gives `GET /api/jobs` all four, and shows the database feature that keeps it fast: **indexes**.
The query parameters

The contract is `GET /api/jobs?q=bank&status=applied&sort=company&page=2&limit=10`. Everything is optional, and everything arrives as text in `req.query`. The controller below turns those texts into a MongoDB filter and options.
Reading the controller

items: **Page and limit** are parsed with `parseInt` and clamped: the page is at least 1, the limit between 1 and 50. Clamping matters: without it a client could ask for `limit=1000000` and make your server fetch the whole collection into memory.
**Status** is only used if it is one of the known values. Anything else is ignored rather than passed to the database.

**Search** builds a case-insensitive regular expression over company, role and location with `$or`. The text is passed through `escapeRegex` first. Without it a visitor typing `C++` or `(` would break the pattern, and a crafted pattern could make the database do a lot of work (a *ReDoS* style attack). Escaping turns every special character into a literal one.
**Sort** uses a lookup table, `SORTS`. The client sends a name such as `company`, and only names in the table work. Never pass a client-supplied value directly as a sort key.
**The answer** includes `items`, `page`, `limit`, `total` and `pages`, so the client can draw page buttons without a second request.

content.text: Notice `Promise.all([find..., countDocuments(...)])`. The page of items and the total are independent questions, so they run at the same time, using the idea from lesson 4. `skip((page - 1) * limit).limit(limit)` is the classic way to paginate. It is simple and fine for thousands of documents. For very large collections, where skipping many documents becomes slow, teams switch to “cursor” pagination based on the last id seen.
Indexes

Without an index, MongoDB answers “newest first” by looking at **every** document and sorting them (a *collection scan*). With an index on `createdAt`, it already has them in order and just reads the first page. An index is a separate, sorted structure that costs a little space and a little time on every write, but makes the matching reads dramatically faster. The second index, on `status` then `createdAt`, serves the very common question “only this status, newest first”.

A useful rule: build indexes for the queries your app actually runs, and put the field you *filter by equality* first and the field you *sort by* last. In lesson 22 both indexes will start with `user`, because every query will begin “this person's jobs”. You can ask MongoDB how it ran a query with `.explain('executionStats')` and look for `IXSCAN` (index used) versus `COLLSCAN` (everything read).

A regular expression search such as the one above cannot use an ordinary index for a middle-of-text match, so it scans. That is fine for a personal tracker where each person has hundreds of jobs. For large-scale text search, use a text index or a dedicated search service.
Fake data to try it on
Your task

items: Run `npm run seed` to add 30 jobs, then try `GET /api/jobs?limit=5&page=3`.
Search for `bank`, then filter with `status=interview`, then combine them.
Try `limit=9999` and `page=-4`. What does the server do?
Search for `c++` and for `(`. Confirm there is no error. Then temporarily remove `escapeRegex` and try again.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `total` and `pages` change with the filters.
Out-of-range values are clamped, not an error or a crash.
Special characters in the search box work as plain text.

content.text: Summary

items: Filter, search, sort and paginate on the server, and always clamp and whitelist what the client sends.
Escape user text before putting it in a regular expression.
Index the fields you filter and sort on; check with `explain`.

faqs.q: What is an index in MongoDB?
faqs.a: A separate sorted structure that lets the database find or order documents without reading every one. It speeds up reads and slightly slows writes, so add indexes for the queries you really run.

faqs.q: Why escape the search text?
faqs.a: Because a regular expression treats characters such as ( + * ? specially. Unescaped, a visitor's search could throw an error or be crafted to make the database do expensive work. Escaping makes them plain characters.

faqs.q: Is skip and limit pagination good enough?
faqs.a: For thousands of documents, yes. For very large collections skip becomes slow because the database still walks past the skipped documents. Then use cursor-based pagination, filtering by the last seen id or date.

The server turns them into a filter. Search text is escaped, so it cannot be used as a regex attack.
An index lets MongoDB jump to matching documents instead of reading all of them.
skip and limit return one page, and the total count tells the client how many pages there are.
The limit is capped, so nobody can ask for a million rows at once.

lessons.title: MongoDB Aggregation: Count Jobs per Status for a Statistics Endpoint
lessons.description: Use an aggregation pipeline to group and count inside the database, fill in missing statuses, compute an honest percentage and avoid the route-order bug.

content.text: The dashboard will show numbers: how many jobs in total, how many per status, and what share of applications reached an interview. You could fetch every job and count in JavaScript, but that moves all the data across the network to count it. A database is built to count quickly where the data lives. MongoDB's tool for that is the **aggregation pipeline**.
What a pipeline is

A pipeline is a list of **stages**. Documents flow through the stages one after another, and each stage changes them: `$match` keeps some, `$group` combines them, `$sort` orders them, `$project` reshapes them, `$limit` cuts them. It is like a conveyor belt with a worker at each station, and it is the same idea as chaining `filter`, `map` and `reduce` on an array, but run inside the database.
Reading the controller

items: `{ $group: { _id: '$status', count: { $sum: 1 } } }` creates one output document per distinct `status` and adds 1 for every job that has it. The text `'$status'` (with a dollar sign) means *the value of the field `status`*.

The result only has statuses that exist. If nobody has an `offer` yet, there is no `offer` row, and a screen that expects it would show a hole. So the code starts from an object with every status set to `0` and then fills in the counts. Designing the answer so the client never has to guess is good API manners.

`interviewRate` is the share of *applications* that reached an interview or an offer. The word is chosen carefully: the denominator excludes jobs that are only `saved`, because you have not applied to those. And when there are no applications, the rate is `null` rather than `0%`, because zero would claim something false. Showing “–” on screen is more honest than showing a number that means nothing yet.

content.text: A statistic is only useful if it is true to what it says. “Interview rate” here is a personal measure of one person's search, not a promise about anyone's chances, and the screen should never present it as more than that.
The route-order bug

Look at the comment next to `/stats`. Express checks routes in order, and `/:id` matches **any** one-segment path. If `/stats` came after `/:id`, a request for `/api/jobs/stats` would be treated as a job whose id is `stats`, and `checkId` would answer `404`. This bug is easy to create and confusing to see, so remember the rule from lesson 9: put specific routes before general ones.
Other pipeline stages worth knowing

items: `$match` first, as early as possible, so later stages see fewer documents (and can use indexes). In lesson 22 the first stage will be `$match: { user: ... }`.
`$sort` and `$limit` for “top 5” questions.
`$lookup` to join another collection, `$unwind` to turn an array into one document per item, and `$addFields` to compute new fields.
`$dateToString` and `$group` together give counts per month: a nice next feature.

content.text: Your task

items: Run `npm run seed` if you have not, then call `GET /api/jobs/stats`.
Move the `/stats` route below `/:id` and call it again. Read the answer, then put it back.
Add the average number of jobs per week. Hint: use `$group` on `$dateToString` or on the week of `createdAt`.
Add `byLocation`: the three places with the most jobs, using `$group`, `$sort` and `$limit`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `byStatus` has all five statuses, with zeros where there are none.
`interviewRate` is `null` for an empty tracker and a whole number otherwise.

content.text: Summary

items: An aggregation pipeline passes documents through stages such as `$match`, `$group` and `$sort` inside the database.
Fill in missing groups so the client never has holes; use `null` for undefined ratios.
Register specific routes (`/stats`) before `/:id`.

faqs.q: When should I use aggregation instead of counting in JavaScript?
faqs.a: Almost always for totals and groups, because the database counts where the data lives and only sends the small result. Fetching every document to count it in JavaScript wastes time and memory.

faqs.q: What does $sum: 1 do in $group?
faqs.a: It adds one for every document in the group, which counts them. To add up a field instead, use $sum with the field name, for example $sum: "$salary".

faqs.q: Why is interviewRate null sometimes?
faqs.a: Because with no applications there is nothing to divide by, and showing 0% would claim that none of your applications led anywhere. Null lets the screen show a dash, which is the honest answer.

lessons.keywords: mongodb aggregation pipeline, mongodb group count, mongoose aggregate, express statistics endpoint

steps.say: Sometimes we need numbers about the data, not the documents themselves.
An aggregation is a pipeline: each stage gets the output of the stage before it.
$match keeps only the jobs we want, here the ones that belong to the user.
$group puts them into buckets by status and counts each bucket.
We shape the result into a simple object, and add an interview rate, for the dashboard.

lessons.title: User Registration and Password Hashing with bcrypt
lessons.description: Create the User model, hash passwords so they are never stored as text, validate the email, and handle duplicate accounts with a 409 answer.

content.text: So far anyone can read and change every job. The Job Tracker needs accounts, so each person sees only their own jobs. That requires two ideas that are often confused. **Authentication** answers “who are you?”. **Authorization** answers “what are you allowed to do?”. This lesson and the next two build authentication; lesson 22 adds the authorization rule that keeps people apart.
We start with the part that has the largest cost if you get it wrong: storing passwords. The rule is absolute. **Never store a password.** Store a *hash* of it.
What a hash is, and why bcrypt

A **hash function** turns any text into a fixed-length scramble, and it only works in one direction: you can get from the password to the hash, but not back. To check a login, you hash what the person typed and compare it with the stored hash. If a thief steals your database, they get hashes, not passwords.

But ordinary fast hashes (such as SHA-256) can be guessed at billions per second by a modern graphics card. Password hashing needs the opposite: it must be **deliberately slow**. **bcrypt** was designed for that. It adds a random **salt** to each password, so two people with the same password get different hashes, and it has a **cost** setting that makes each guess take real time. We use `bcryptjs`, a pure JavaScript version that installs everywhere without compiling anything.

items: **`email`** is `lowercase` and `trim`med, so `Ana@Example.com ` and `ana@example.com` are the same account, and `unique: true` creates a unique **index** so MongoDB itself refuses a second account with the same email.
**`match`** is a light format check. Do not try to validate email addresses perfectly with a regular expression; the only real proof an address works is sending a message to it (a feature for later).
**`select: false`** on `passwordHash` means that queries do not return it unless you explicitly ask with `.select('+passwordHash')`. A forgotten `.select` can then never leak it.
The `toJSON` transform deletes `passwordHash` as a second safety net, in case a document with the hash ever gets sent.

content.text: The register controller

The password is checked **before** hashing: at least 8 characters, and at most 72. The upper limit is a bcrypt detail: it only reads the first 72 bytes, so a longer password adds nothing, and a very long one wastes server time. `bcrypt.hash(password, 12)` produces the hash. The number 12 is the **cost**: each increase of 1 doubles the time. Around 10 to 12 is common today, and it should be raised over the years as computers get faster.

`User.create` fails if the email already exists, and MongoDB reports that with the error code `11000`. The error handler from lesson 17 turns that into `409 Conflict` with a message for the `email` field, so a registration form can show “That email is already used”.

Do not put a minimum like “must contain a symbol” and a maximum like 12 characters. Long passphrases are stronger than short complicated ones. Guidance from security organisations favours length, allowing every character, and checking against lists of known leaked passwords where possible.
Your task

items: Run `npm install` in `server` (it adds `bcryptjs`), then register with `POST /api/auth/register` and a JSON body of name, email and password.
Look at the `users` collection in Atlas. Find the `passwordHash` and see that it starts with `$2a$12$`.
Register the same email again. What status do you get? Try `ANA@example.com` in capitals.
Register the same password for two different emails and compare the two hashes. Why are they different?

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A good registration answers 201 with the user and no `passwordHash`.
A short password answers 400 with a message for `password`.
A repeated email answers 409.

content.text: Summary

items: Authentication is who you are; authorization is what you may do.
Store a slow, salted hash (bcrypt), never the password.
Make emails lowercase and unique; hide the hash by default and in JSON.

faqs.q: Why not encrypt passwords instead of hashing them?
faqs.a: Encryption can be reversed with the key, so a thief who gets the key and the data gets every password. A hash cannot be reversed. You only ever need to check a guess against it, never to read the original.

faqs.q: What is the bcrypt cost factor?
faqs.a: It controls how slow hashing is. Each increase of 1 doubles the time. Pick a value that takes roughly a tenth of a second or more on your server (10 to 12 is common) and raise it as hardware improves.

faqs.q: Why bcryptjs and not bcrypt?
faqs.a: bcryptjs is pure JavaScript and installs on any system with no build tools. The native bcrypt package is faster but needs compilation. For most apps the difference does not matter. The hashes are compatible.

steps.say: A person sends an email and a password.
The server checks the email format and a sensible password length first.
The password is run through bcrypt: a one-way function with a random salt, made slow on purpose.
Only the hash is saved. Even we cannot read the password back, and a stolen database does not give the passwords away.
The reply never includes the hash. A duplicate email gives a clear conflict error.

lessons.title: Login with JWT: Sign In, Issue a Token and Avoid Timing Leaks
lessons.description: How JSON Web Tokens work, how to sign and verify them, and how to write a login that gives the same answer for a wrong email and a wrong password.

content.text: The person has an account. Now they must prove who they are, and your server must remember that for the next request. HTTP has no memory: each request stands alone. So after a correct login the server hands the client a **token**: a small piece of text that the client sends back with every later request, like a wristband at an event.
What a JWT is

A **JSON Web Token** has three parts separated by dots: a *header*, a *payload* and a *signature*. The payload holds claims such as “the user id is 64f... and this expires in seven days”. The signature is made with a secret that only your server knows. When a token comes back, the server recomputes the signature: if the payload was changed, or the token was made by someone without the secret, the signature will not match and the token is rejected.

The payload of a JWT is encoded, **not encrypted**. Anyone who holds the token can read it by pasting it into a decoder. Never put passwords, emails you want private or other sensitive data in it. Put only what you need, usually the user id. The security is in the signature.

`jwt.sign(payload, secret, { expiresIn })` creates a token. We store the user id in `sub` (short for “subject”), a standard claim name. `jwt.verify(token, secret)` returns the payload or throws if the token is invalid or expired. The function `secret()` refuses to run when `JWT_SECRET` is missing, because a missing secret would silently make every token forgeable.

# Copy this file to .env and fill it in. Never commit .env to Git.
PORT=5000
CLIENT_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
MONGODB_URI=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/job_tracker
# Make a long random secret with:  node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))"
JWT_SECRET=change-me-to-a-long-random-string
JWT_EXPIRES_IN=7d

Make the secret long and random, as the comment in the file shows. If it is guessable, anyone can create tokens for any user. If you change it, every existing token stops working, which is a handy emergency button after a leak.
The login controller

items: **The same message for both failures.** If the answer were “no such email” for one and “wrong password” for the other, an attacker could use the form to find out which emails have accounts (called *user enumeration*). So both cases answer `401 Email or password is wrong`.

**The same time for both failures.** Comparing a password with bcrypt takes noticeable time, while “no such user” would return instantly, and that difference can be measured. So when the email is unknown we still call `bcrypt.compare` against a throw-away `DUMMY_HASH`. This is the idea behind a *timing attack* defence.
**`.select('+passwordHash')`** is how we ask for the hash that is hidden by default.
**Type checks.** `typeof email === 'string'` stops a client from sending an object instead of text. Lesson 23 will explain why that matters.
**Register now also returns a token**, so a new person is signed in straight away.

content.text: Where does the client keep the token?

The React app (lesson 32) will keep the token in `localStorage` and send it in an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. This is simple and common, and it has a known trade-off: JavaScript on the page can read `localStorage`, so a cross-site scripting (XSS) bug could steal the token. The alternative, an `httpOnly` cookie, cannot be read by scripts but needs protection against cross-site request forgery. Neither is free. For this course we use the header approach and keep the pages free of unsafe HTML; lesson 40 lists the cookie version as a next step.
Your task

items: Run `npm install` in `server` (adds `jsonwebtoken`). Add a long `JWT_SECRET` to `.env`.
Log in with the right password and copy the token. Paste it into a JWT decoder and read the payload: find `sub`, `iat` (issued at) and `exp` (expires).
Change one character of the token and try to `jwt.verify` it in a small script. What error do you get?
Log in with a wrong email and with a wrong password. Compare the status, message and the time taken.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A correct login answers 200 with `token` and `user`.
Wrong email and wrong password give the same 401 message.
The decoded token shows `sub` and an expiry but no password or email.

content.text: Summary

items: A JWT is signed, not secret: store only the user id and an expiry in it.
Sign with a long random secret from `.env`; verify on every request.
Answer wrong email and wrong password identically, and take the same time doing it.

faqs.q: Is a JWT encrypted?
faqs.a: No. It is signed, so it cannot be changed without detection, but anyone holding it can read the payload. Keep sensitive data out of it.

faqs.q: How long should a token last?
faqs.a: Short enough that a stolen one stops working soon, long enough that people are not signed out all the time. Seven days is a common simple choice for small apps. Bigger systems use short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens.

faqs.q: Why not say "email not found" on login?
faqs.a: It tells an attacker which email addresses have accounts, which helps phishing and guessing. A single message for every failure reveals nothing.

lessons.title: Protect Routes and Keep Users Apart: Auth Middleware and Ownership Checks
lessons.description: Write auth middleware, link every job to its owner, and prove that one person cannot read or change another person's jobs.

content.text: Tokens exist. Now every private route must require one, and each query must be limited to the person it belongs to. This lesson contains the most important rule of the whole project, stated in lesson 6: **a person can only ever see and change their own jobs**. Authentication alone does not give you that. Many real data leaks come from apps that check *that* you are signed in, but not *whose* data you are asking for.
The protect middleware

items: It reads the `Authorization` header, expects the form `Bearer <token>`, and answers `401` if it is missing.
`verifyToken` throws for a forged or expired token; we turn that into a `401` with a helpful message.
`User.findById(payload.sub)` loads the person. If the account was deleted after the token was issued, we refuse, so tokens of deleted accounts are useless.
On success it puts the user on `req.user` and calls `next()`. Every later function can say `req.user._id` and know it came from a verified token, not from anything the client typed.

content.text: Notice that this `async` middleware throws `HttpError` and does not call `next(err)` itself. Express 5 forwards the rejection to the error handler for you.
Linking jobs to users

`user: { type: ObjectId, ref: 'User', required: true, index: true }` is a **reference**: it stores the owner's `_id`. The `ref` tells Mongoose which model it points to, so later you could use `.populate('user')` to fetch the owner's details. The `toJSON` transform now also deletes `user`, because the client does not need it. The indexes from lesson 18 now start with `user`, because every query now begins with “this person's jobs”.
Scoping every query

Read the changes against lesson 18. The list starts its filter with `{ user: req.user._id }`. Reading, updating and deleting one job use `findOne({ _id, user })`, `findOneAndUpdate({ _id, user }, ...)` and `findOneAndDelete({ _id, user })`. If the id belongs to someone else, the result is `null` and the answer is `404`, exactly as if the job did not exist. We use `404` rather than `403` on purpose: a `403` would confirm to a stranger that the id exists.

And in `createJob`, the owner is added by the server: `{ ...pickJobFields(req.body), user: req.user._id }`. The owner is **never** read from the body. If it were, a client could create jobs in someone else's account by sending `"user": "..."`. `pickJobFields` already drops that field, and putting `user` after the spread makes the rule impossible to break by accident.

The statistics controller shows a subtle detail. In an aggregation, Mongoose does **not** convert an id string to an ObjectId for you, so `$match` needs the real `ObjectId`. `req.user._id` already is one, which is another reason to take the id from the loaded user and not from a string.

`router.use(protect)` at the top applies the middleware to every route below it, so a new route added later is protected by default. Secure by default is safer than remembering to add a guard each time. The auth router uses `protect` only on `GET /me`, which returns the signed-in user and is what the React app calls to restore a session.
Proving it works

The updated smoke script (and `requests.http`) now registers two people, Ana and Ben. Ana creates a job. Ben tries to read, change and delete it and must get `404` each time. This is the test that matters most in the whole project. Add something like it for every resource you ever build.

`npm run seed` now creates a demo account `demo@example.com` with the password `Demo12345` and 30 jobs. The React lessons use it until the real login screen arrives in lesson 32. It is for local learning only: never create a known account like this on a real server.
Your task

items: Run `npm run seed`, then `npm run smoke` against your running server.
Call `GET /api/jobs` with no token, with a made-up token, and with a real one. Compare the answers.
Create a job as one user. Copy its id, and request it with another user's token. What status do you get?
Try to create a job with `"user": "<another user's id>"` in the body. Check in the database which user owns it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The smoke script passes all of its checks, including “another user cannot read Ana's job (404)”.
A token for a deleted user is refused.

content.text: Summary

items: `protect` verifies the token and puts the user on `req.user`.
Every query includes the owner; the owner comes from the token, never the body.
Answer 404 for someone else's data, and apply `protect` with `router.use` so new routes are safe by default.

faqs.q: Why not return 403 for another user's job?
faqs.a: 403 tells the caller the thing exists but is forbidden, which leaks information. Answering 404 treats it as if it does not exist for them. Use 403 when the resource is known to the user but an action is not allowed.

faqs.q: Is checking the token enough to protect data?
faqs.a: No. It proves who is asking. You must also make every query only touch data that belongs to that person (or that their role allows). Missing the second step is a very common cause of data leaks.

faqs.q: What does router.use(protect) do?
faqs.a: It adds protect as middleware for every route defined after it on that router, so all of them require a valid token. Routes added later are protected automatically.

The protect middleware verifies the token and loads the user. No token or a bad one gives 401.

lessons.title: Express Security Basics: helmet, Rate Limiting, NoSQL Injection and Config Checks
lessons.description: Add safe HTTP headers, slow down password guessing, refuse MongoDB operator objects in input, and fail at start when configuration is missing.

content.text: A working login is not a secure login. Real APIs are scanned and attacked within hours of going online, usually by automated scripts, not by someone who knows your app. This lesson adds four protections, each small, that stop the most common automated attacks. None of them is a substitute for the ones you already have (hashing, token checks, ownership), and together they make a solid base.
1. Safe headers with helmet

`helmet()` is one line that sets a group of HTTP response headers that tell browsers to behave safely: do not guess content types (`X-Content-Type-Options`), do not allow your pages inside frames on other sites (clickjacking), only use HTTPS, and apply a Content Security Policy. It also removes the `X-Powered-By: Express` header that advertises your technology. It is cheap, it rarely causes problems, and it is the first thing a security review looks for.
2. Rate limiting

Without a limit, a script can try thousands of passwords a minute against `/api/auth/login`. `express-rate-limit` counts requests per IP address in a time window and answers `429 Too Many Requests` once a person goes over. We apply it to `/api/auth` only (20 attempts per 15 minutes), because that is where guessing happens. `standardHeaders` tells the client how many tries remain.

One production detail catches many people. Behind nginx or a host's load balancer, every request appears to come from the proxy's address, so *everyone shares one limit*. Setting `TRUST_PROXY=1` tells Express to read the real visitor address from the `X-Forwarded-For` header. Only set it when you really are behind one proxy; otherwise a visitor could fake the header.
3. NoSQL injection

In SQL, the famous attack is typing `' OR 1=1 --` into a form. MongoDB has a cousin. Remember that filters use operator objects like `{ $gt: '' }`. If your login does `User.findOne({ email: req.body.email })` and a client sends the JSON `{ "email": { "$gt": "" } }`, the filter becomes “email greater than empty text”, which matches the first user. The attacker never needed an email.

Two defences are used together. First, **check types**: lesson 21's login already refuses anything that is not a `string`. Second, `rejectOperators` in `security.js` walks through the JSON body and refuses any key that starts with `$` or contains a dot, at any depth. Our app never needs such keys from clients, so refusing them is safe.
4. Fail at start when configuration is wrong

`checkEnv` stops the server immediately, with a clear message, if `MONGODB_URI` or `JWT_SECRET` is missing, and, in production, if the secret is short or still has the example value. A server that starts with a missing secret and then fails on the first login is much harder to debug than one that refuses to start.
A short security checklist

items: Hash passwords; use long random secrets from `.env`.
Check the token **and** the owner on every private route.
Validate and whitelist all input; clamp numbers; escape text used in regular expressions.
Limit request size (`express.json({ limit })`) and request rate.
Keep dependencies updated; run `npm audit` now and then and read what it says before changing anything.
Never log passwords, tokens or full request bodies.

content.text: Security is a process, not a feature. This course shows the fundamentals that stop the most common problems. For an app that holds sensitive data, add an independent security review.
Your task

items: Run `npm install` in `server` (adds `helmet` and `express-rate-limit`). Restart and call any route with `curl -i` to see the new headers.
Send eleven wrong logins in a row with `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT=10` set in `.env`. Which request is the first to answer 429?
Send `{ "email": { "$gt": "" }, "password": "x" }` to login. What do you get?
Remove `JWT_SECRET` from `.env` and start the server. Read the message.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Responses carry `X-Content-Type-Options` and no `X-Powered-By`.
The 11th wrong login within the window answers 429.
The operator-object login answers 400.

content.text: Summary

items: helmet sets safe headers; rate limiting slows guessing; operator objects are refused.
Behind a proxy set `TRUST_PROXY=1` so limits use real visitor addresses.
Fail fast at start when required settings are missing.

faqs.q: What is NoSQL injection?
faqs.a: Sending a MongoDB operator object, such as { "$gt": "" }, where the code expects text, so that the query matches more than intended. Defend by checking input types and refusing keys that start with $.

faqs.q: Does helmet make my app secure?
faqs.a: It makes browsers handle your responses more safely and removes some information leaks. It does not replace authentication, validation or authorization. Think of it as one inexpensive layer.

faqs.q: Why does the rate limit need TRUST_PROXY behind nginx?
faqs.a: Behind a proxy every request seems to come from the proxy's IP address, so all visitors would share one limit. TRUST_PROXY tells Express to use the forwarded visitor address instead.

lessons.title: Automated API Tests with the Built-in Node.js Test Runner
lessons.description: Split app from server so tests can start the app, run against a throw-away database, and check authentication, ownership, validation and pagination.

content.text: A smoke script is a good start, but you have to remember to run it, and it only covers one path. **Automated tests** run all your checks with one command, in a clean database, and fail loudly the moment a change breaks something. They are what lets you change code next month without fear. Since Node.js 20 the test runner is built in (`node:test`), so you need no extra library.
Step 1: separate the app from the server

Until now `index.js` built the app **and** started it. A test must not start a server on port 5000 or connect to your real database. So the app moves into `app.js`, which only builds and exports it, and `index.js` becomes a small file that checks the config, connects and calls `listen`. A test can now `import { app }`, start it on a random free port with `app.listen(0)`, and connect to a different database. This split is a very common structure in real projects.
Step 2: the tests

items: **`describe` and `it`** group and name the checks. Names should read like sentences: “keeps people apart”.
**`before` and `after`** run once around the group. We connect to the **test** database, wipe it, build its indexes, start the app on a random port, and at the end wipe it again and stop.

**`MONGODB_URI_TEST`** is a separate address in `.env`. The tests drop the whole database, so the script refuses to run without it. **Never point it at real data.** (If the variable is missing the file says so and exits cleanly.)
**`assert/strict`** compares values with strict equality (`assert.equal`, `assert.deepEqual`, `assert.ok`).
**A small `api()` helper** wraps `fetch` so each check is short, and `signUp()` makes a fresh user and returns its token.

content.text: One line deserves a note: `Promise.all(Object.values(mongoose.models).map((m) => m.syncIndexes()))`. `dropDatabase()` also deletes the **unique index** on email, and Mongoose only builds indexes when it first sees a model, not again. Without rebuilding it, the “duplicate email” test would pass or fail depending on timing. Tests that sometimes fail for no visible reason (called *flaky*) are worse than no tests, so it pays to find the cause. This one was found while writing this very course.
What to test

Look at the list of checks. The suite covers the **happy path** (register, log in, create, list, update, delete), the **unhappy paths** (wrong password, duplicate email, invalid input, no token, a garbage token), the **security rules** (operator objects refused, one user cannot see another's jobs), and **behaviour** (pagination and statistics). When you add a feature, add its tests in the same change. When you find a bug, write the test that fails first, then fix it.
Tests are code and need the same care. Keep each test independent: one that depends on another's leftovers will break when the order changes. This is why every test above creates its own user.
Run them

Add `MONGODB_URI_TEST=mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/job_tracker_test` (or a separate Atlas database) to `.env`, then run `npm test`. The script `node --test --test-concurrency=1` finds files in a `test` folder, and the concurrency of 1 runs files one at a time so they do not wipe each other's database.
Your task

items: Add `MONGODB_URI_TEST` to `.env` and run `npm test`. Read the report.
Write a test that registering with a 73-character password answers 400.
Write a test that `GET /api/jobs?limit=9999` returns at most 50 items.
Break something on purpose (for example remove `{ user: req.user._id }` from `listJobs`) and watch which test catches it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `npm test` ends with `# fail 0`.
Breaking the owner filter makes “keeps people apart” fail.

content.text: Summary

items: Export the app from `app.js`; start it from `index.js`. Tests import the app.
Use a separate test database and rebuild its indexes after dropping it.
Test happy paths, unhappy paths and security rules; keep every test independent.

faqs.q: Do I need Jest or Mocha?
faqs.a: Not for this project. The built-in node:test runner has describe, it, before, after and assertions. Jest and Vitest offer extra features such as mocking and watch mode, which you can add later if you need them.

faqs.q: Why must tests use a separate database?
faqs.a: Tests create and delete data and here even drop the whole database. Running them against real data would destroy it. Always give tests their own throw-away database address.

faqs.q: What is a flaky test?
faqs.a: A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any change to the code, often because of timing or leftover state. Fix the cause or delete the test, since people stop trusting a suite that cries wolf.

The tests import the app without starting a real server, and send requests to it.

Each test sends a request and asserts the status and the body, including the failure cases.

lessons.title: React and Vite Setup: Components and JSX
lessons.description: Create the React app with Vite, understand how main.jsx starts it, write your first components in JSX, and set up the dev proxy to the Express API.

content.text: The back end is finished enough to be useful. Now the screens. **React** is a library for building user interfaces out of small, reusable pieces called **components**. Instead of finding elements and changing them by hand, you describe what the screen should look like for the current data, and React updates the page to match. This is the biggest idea in React, and the next six lessons build on it.

We use **Vite** to run and build the app. It starts in a moment, reloads the browser as you edit, and produces a small, fast production build. Create React App is no longer the recommended way to start, and Vite is the common replacement.
The files Vite gives you

items: **`index.html`** is the only HTML page. It has an empty `<div id="root">` and loads `main.jsx` as a module. Everything else is drawn by JavaScript.

**`main.jsx`** is the entry point. `createRoot(...).render(<App />)` tells React to take control of the `root` div and draw the `App` component inside it. `StrictMode` runs some checks in development (and runs effects twice on purpose, to help you find bugs).
**`package.json`** lists React, ReactDOM, the Vite plugin for React, and Vite. The scripts are `dev`, `build` and `preview`.

content.text: The proxy to your API

In development the React app runs on port 5173 and the API on 5000. A page on one port that calls another is a cross-origin request, which needs CORS. The `proxy` setting avoids that: Vite forwards any request that starts with `/api` to the Express server, so the browser sees only one address. Your React code can then call `fetch('/api/jobs')` with a plain path, and in production, when Express serves the built app (lesson 38), the same code works without any change.
Components and JSX
A component is a **function that returns JSX**. JSX looks like HTML but is JavaScript underneath: each tag becomes a function call. Four rules cover most of what you need.

items: A component's name starts with a capital letter (`Header`), which is how React tells it from an ordinary HTML tag (`header`).
A component returns **one** root element. Wrap siblings in a parent, or in an empty fragment `<>...</>`.
Use `className` instead of `class`, and `htmlFor` instead of `for`, because `class` and `for` are reserved words in JavaScript.

Put any JavaScript expression inside curly braces: `{year}`, `{items.length}`, `{isOpen ? 'Hide' : 'Show'}`. Statements such as `if` and `for` do not go in braces; use the conditional `? :`, `&&`, or `.map()` for lists.

content.text: `App` is the root component. It renders a `Header`, and two `JobCard`s, using each like an HTML tag. Right now both cards show the same text. In the next lesson, **props** let each card receive its own data. Notice also how the layout is described, not constructed: there is no code that says “create an element and append it”.
The styles
We use one plain CSS file. The custom properties at the top (`--brand` and friends) make colours easy to change in one place. In lesson 34 the file is replaced by a polished responsive version.

Components must be pure during rendering: given the same inputs, return the same JSX, and do not change things outside themselves. Side effects such as fetching data belong in event handlers and in `useEffect`, which come in lessons 26 and 28.
Your task

items: Run `npm run setup` from the project root (or `npm install` inside `client`), then `npm run dev` inside `client`. Open the address Vite prints.
Change the text in `Header.jsx` and save. Watch the browser update without a reload.
Create a `Footer` component that shows the year, and use it in `App`.
Open the browser tools, Network tab, and find the request for `main.jsx`. See how Vite serves your source files in development.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The browser shows the header and two cards.
Editing a component updates the page immediately (this is called hot reloading).

content.text: Summary

items: `index.html` + `main.jsx` start React; `App` is the root component.
A component is a capitalised function returning one JSX element; braces hold JavaScript expressions.
The Vite proxy sends `/api` calls to Express, so the same URLs work in development and production.

faqs.q: Why use Vite instead of Create React App?
faqs.a: Vite starts and reloads much faster and is actively maintained, while Create React App is no longer the recommended starting point. The React code you write is the same either way.

faqs.q: What is JSX?
faqs.a: A syntax that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript. A build step turns each tag into a function call. It is not required, but nearly every React project uses it.

faqs.q: Why does React run my effects twice in development?
faqs.a: StrictMode does it on purpose to help you find effects that are not cleaned up properly. It only happens in development, never in the production build.

lessons.title: React Props, State and Events: useState and Updating Without Mutation
lessons.description: Pass data with props, keep changing data in state, handle events and update state without mutation, with a status picker you can use.

content.text: A screen that never changes is just a page. Real apps respond: you click, type, choose. React gives you three tools for that, and nearly everything else in the library builds on them. **Props** carry data *into* a component. **State** is data that belongs to a component and can *change*. **Events** are how the user's actions reach your code.
Props: inputs for a component

Props are passed like HTML attributes, `<StatusBadge status="applied" />`, and received as one object, which we usually destructure right in the parameter list: `function StatusBadge({ status })`. Props are **read only**. A component must never change its own props, because they belong to its parent. If something has to change, the parent changes it and passes new props down.

`JobCard` now receives two props: a `job` object, and a function `onStatusChange`. Passing a function as a prop is the way a child tells its parent that something happened. The card does not know how the list is stored, and it does not need to. This is the pattern: **data flows down as props; events flow up as function calls**.
State: data that changes

`const [jobs, setJobs] = useState(SAMPLE)` creates a piece of state. `useState` returns a pair: the current value, and a function that sets a new one. When you call the setter, React remembers the new value and **runs the component again** to draw the screen for it. You never edit the page by hand. You change the state and the page follows.
Never change state in place

The most important rule in this lesson: **do not mutate state.** `jobs[0].status = 'offer'` followed by `setJobs(jobs)` does nothing useful, because React checks whether the value is *a different one* and finds the same array. You must give it a new array and new objects for what changed. That is why lesson 3 taught spread and `map`.

Notice that the setter was given a **function** `(current) => ...`. Use that form whenever the new state depends on the old one. It always receives the latest value, even if several updates happen close together, which a plain `setJobs(jobs.map(...))` can miss.
Events

Attach a handler with a camel-case prop: `onClick`, `onChange`, `onSubmit`. You pass the **function itself**, not the result of calling it: `onClick={save}` is right, `onClick={save()}` runs `save` during drawing and is a bug. For inputs, `e.target.value` holds what the person typed. In `JobCard`, the `<select>`'s `onChange` calls the parent's function with the job id and the chosen status.
Keys

When you draw a list with `.map()`, give every item a **`key`** that is stable and unique among its siblings: here `key={job.id}`. React uses keys to tell which item is which when the list changes, so it keeps the right state with the right item. Do not use the array index as a key for lists that can be reordered or have items removed.
State is **per component instance** and is lost when the component is removed from the page. Data that must survive a refresh belongs on the server (lesson 28 onwards) or in browser storage.
Your task

items: Run the app. Change a job's status with the dropdown and watch the badge colour change.
Add a state variable `showOnlyActive` and a checkbox that hides jobs whose status is `rejected`. Use `.filter()` while drawing; do not delete from the array.
Add a button to each card that cycles the status to the next one in the list.
Open React Developer Tools (a browser extension) and look at the state of `App` while you click.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Choosing a status changes only that card.
You can explain why `setJobs((current) => ...)` is safer than `setJobs(jobs.map(...))`.

content.text: Summary

items: Props flow down and are read only; functions passed as props let children report events up.
`useState` gives a value and a setter; calling the setter redraws the component.
Never mutate state: create new arrays and objects, and give list items stable keys.

faqs.q: What is the difference between props and state?
faqs.a: Props are inputs a component receives from its parent and must not change. State is data the component owns and can change. When state changes React draws the component again.

faqs.q: Why does my state not update when I change an object?
faqs.a: React compares by reference. If you edit the same object and set it again, it looks unchanged. Create a new object or array (spread, map, filter) and set that instead.

faqs.q: Why do list items need keys?
faqs.a: Keys let React match old and new items when a list changes, so it can keep the right state and DOM with the right item. Use a stable unique id, not the index, when items can move or be removed.

lessons.title: React Lists and Forms: Controlled Inputs, Validation and Accessible Labels
lessons.description: Build the job form with controlled inputs, validate before sending, show errors next to fields, and make the form usable with a keyboard and a screen reader.

content.text: Forms are where most web apps spend most of their time, and where most bugs and accessibility problems live. In React the standard approach is the **controlled input**: the input's value always comes from state, and every keystroke goes back into state. React is then the single source of truth, so you can validate, reset or change what is shown at any moment.
The form component

items: **`values`** holds what is in the fields. **`errors`** holds a message per field. Both are state.

**One `change` function for all fields.** Each input has a `name` that matches a key in `values`, so `e.target.name` says which field changed, and `[e.target.name]: e.target.value` is a *computed key* that updates it. That avoids one handler per field.
**`e.preventDefault()`** in `submit` stops the browser's default of sending the form and reloading the page.

**`noValidate`** on the form turns off the browser's pop-up bubbles so that our own messages, which can match the site's style and language, are used. The server validates too (lesson 12), so nothing depends on this.

content.text: Accessibility is not optional
Several small details here make the form usable by everybody, and they cost almost nothing.

items: Every input has a **`<label htmlFor>`** that matches the input's `id`. Clicking the label focuses the field, and screen readers announce it. Placeholder text is not a label: it disappears when you type.
**`aria-invalid`** marks a field with a problem, and the red border uses the same attribute in CSS, so the visual and the semantic state cannot drift apart.
Error text sits right under its field. For messages that appear after an action, the next lessons add `role="alert"` so screen readers announce them.
Use a real `<button type="submit">` inside a real `<form>`: Enter then submits the form for free.

content.text: Using the form and drawing the list

`App` gives the form an `onSubmit` function and adds the new job to the list with a spread: `[{ ...values, id: Date.now() }, ...cur]`. The list is drawn with `.map()` and a `key`. Notice the three states of the list: items exist; nothing exists yet (we show a friendly message); and, in lesson 28, loading. Always design all three, because an empty screen with no explanation looks like a bug.
The job is still only added to the **screen**. Reload the page and it is gone. Saving it on the server is lesson 31. Doing it in steps keeps each idea clear.
Where should state live?

A common beginner question is where to put state. A good rule is: **put it in the closest component that needs it, and lift it up only when two siblings need to share it.** The form's `values` are only used by the form, so they live there. The list of jobs is used by the list and by the form's submit handler, so it lives in `App`, their common parent.
Do not store values that you can calculate from other state. `jobs.length` is derived from `jobs`, so calculate it while drawing instead of keeping a separate `count` that can fall out of step.
Your task

items: Run the app. Submit the empty form and read the errors. Fix one field and submit again.
Use the keyboard only: tab through the fields, choose a status with the arrow keys, and submit with Enter.
Add a `Pay` field (`salaryNote`) and a `Notes` textarea to the form.
Add a check that blocks company names longer than 120 characters, with a message.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Errors appear under the fields and clear when the form is valid.
A new job appears at the top and the form resets.
You can complete the whole flow without a mouse.

content.text: Summary

items: A controlled input reads its value from state and writes every change back.
One `onChange` with computed keys can serve all fields.
Labels, `aria-invalid` and real buttons make a form usable for everyone.

faqs.q: What is a controlled input?
faqs.a: An input whose value is set by React state and updated on every change event. React is the single source of truth, which makes validation, resetting and conditional logic simple.

faqs.q: Why not use the browser's built-in validation?
faqs.a: You can, and it is a good fallback. Custom validation lets you control the wording, placement and styling, and matches the server's messages. In either case the server must validate again.

faqs.q: Is a placeholder enough as a label?
faqs.a: No. A placeholder disappears when you type and is not reliably announced by screen readers. Use a visible label connected with htmlFor and id.

lessons.title: useEffect and Fetching Data from Your API: Loading, Errors and Cleanup
lessons.description: Call the Express API from React, handle loading and error states, cancel requests that are no longer needed, and write a small api() helper.

content.text: The screen so far shows made-up data. Time to connect React to the API you built. Fetching data is a **side effect**: something that reaches outside the component. React gives you the hook `useEffect` for that. It runs your code **after** the component has been drawn, and lets you clean up afterwards.
One place for talking to the API

items: `api(path, options)` adds the `/api` prefix, the JSON header and the `Authorization` token, so no component repeats that.

It throws an `ApiError` with the **status**, the **message** and the field **details** from the server whenever the answer is not OK. Remember that `fetch` itself does not fail on 400 or 500 (lesson 4).
`204 No Content` returns `null`, because there is no body to parse.
The token is read from `localStorage`. Lesson 32 sets it when the person signs in.

content.text: useEffect

`useEffect(fn, [dependencies])` runs `fn` after drawing. The **dependency array** controls when it runs again. With `[]` it runs once, when the component first appears. With `[id]` it runs again whenever `id` changes. With no array it runs after every draw, which is rarely what you want. The rule that avoids most bugs: **list every value from the component that the effect uses.**

The function you return from the effect is its **cleanup**. It runs before the next run and when the component disappears. Here we use it to call `controller.abort()`. An `AbortController` cancels a request that is no longer needed, for example when the person leaves the page before the answer arrives. Without it, the late answer would try to update a component that no longer exists, or, worse, an older request could finish **after** a newer one and show stale data (a *race condition*).
Three states: loading, error, data

Network calls take time and can fail. The component keeps three pieces of state, `jobs`, `loading` and `error`, and draws something sensible for each. A blank screen is not an acceptable loading state, and a silent failure is not an acceptable error state. The error message ends with a hint about the likely cause, which saves a beginner a lot of time.

For this lesson only, the effect signs in as the demo account created by `npm run seed` so that a token exists. This is **temporary**, and lesson 32 replaces it with real sign-in pages. Never ship a hard-coded login.

The effect cannot be an `async` function directly, because it must return either nothing or a cleanup function, and an `async` function returns a promise. So we define an `async function load()` inside and call it, as the file shows.
What about the form?

It still only changes the screen, and is marked with a comment. Saving through the API comes in lesson 31, after you have met routing and shared state. Reload the page and the form's jobs disappear, while the server's jobs return. That difference is worth seeing with your own eyes.
Your task

items: Start the server, run `npm run seed`, then start the client. You should see 30 jobs from your database.
Stop the server and reload. Read the error message. Start it again.
Slow the network in the browser's Network tab (choose “Slow 3G”) and watch the loading message.
Add `console.log('effect ran')` inside the effect. Why does it print twice in development? (Hint: lesson 25.)

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The list shows the jobs from MongoDB.
With the server stopped, a clear error replaces the list.
Reloading brings back the saved jobs, not the ones you added on screen.

content.text: Summary

items: Wrap `fetch` in one `api()` helper that sets headers and throws `ApiError`.
`useEffect` runs after drawing; the dependency array says when to run again; the returned function cleans up.
Always draw loading, error and empty states.

faqs.q: Why can't I make useEffect's callback async?
faqs.a: An effect must return nothing or a cleanup function. An async function always returns a promise, which React would treat as an invalid cleanup. Define an async function inside the effect and call it.

faqs.q: What goes in the dependency array?
faqs.a: Every value from the component (props, state, functions) that the effect reads. An empty array means "run once on mount". Leaving values out causes stale data bugs.

faqs.q: Why abort requests in the cleanup?
faqs.a: To avoid updating state after the component is gone and to prevent a slow old request from overwriting a newer answer. AbortController cancels the fetch when the effect cleans up.

lessons.title: React Router: Pages, Links, URL Parameters and a Shared Layout
lessons.description: Turn one screen into several pages with React Router 7: routes, a layout with an Outlet, NavLink, useParams and a catch-all 404 page.

content.text: One screen is not an app. We want a list page, a page for one job, and later sign-in pages, each with its own address that can be bookmarked and shared. A **single page application** (SPA) does this without reloading: **React Router** watches the address bar and draws the right component, and links change the address without asking the server for a new page.
Set up the router
`BrowserRouter` wraps the app and makes the current address available to everything below it. The `react-router-dom` package is added in `package.json`; run `npm install` after you copy it.
Declare the routes

items: `<Routes>` picks the **best matching** route for the current address.
`<Route index element={<JobsPage />} />` is the page at the parent's own path (`/`).
`path="jobs/:id"` has a **parameter**: `/jobs/64f...` matches, and the part after `/jobs/` is called `id`.
`path="*"` matches everything else, so unknown addresses get your own 404 page and not a blank screen.
The routes are **nested** inside `<Route element={<Layout />}>`. A route without a path that only has an element is a *layout route*.

content.text: A layout with an Outlet

`<Outlet />` is the hole where the matching child page is drawn. The header stays on screen while the page under it changes. Nothing is reloaded, and the header is not drawn again from scratch. In lesson 32 the same idea gives us a `ProtectedRoute` that wraps all private pages.

`<NavLink>` is a link that does not reload the page, and it adds the class `active` when it points to the current page, so you can style the current item. The `end` prop makes `/` match only the exact address and not every address that starts with `/`. For links that do not need the active style use `<Link>`. Never use a plain `<a href>` for pages inside your app, because that asks the server for a whole new page.
The list and detail pages

`useParams()` returns the parameters from the address: `const { id } = useParams()`. The detail page fetches that job in an effect that lists `id` in its dependency array. If the person goes straight from one job's address to another, the effect runs again. A `404` from the API is turned into a friendly message with a link back, instead of a raw error.

A single page application needs the **server** to cooperate. If someone reloads `/jobs/123`, the browser asks the server for exactly that path, which is not a real file. In development Vite handles this. In production lesson 38 makes Express answer every non-API path with `index.html`.
Your task

items: Run `npm install` in `client` and open the app. Click “Open details” on a job. Watch the address change and notice that the page does not reload.
Use the browser's back and forward buttons. They work, because the router uses the history API.
Type a wrong address such as `/nothing`. You should see the 404 page.
Add an `/about` route with a simple page and a `NavLink` for it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The address changes without a full reload.
The header stays while the page changes.
Unknown addresses show your 404 page.

content.text: Summary

items: `BrowserRouter`, `Routes` and `Route` map addresses to components; `:id` creates a parameter.
A layout route with `<Outlet />` shares a header across pages.
Use `Link` and `NavLink` for in-app navigation, and add a `*` route for 404.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Link and NavLink?
faqs.a: Both navigate without reloading. NavLink also knows whether it points to the current page and adds an active class (and aria-current), so you can style the current menu item.

faqs.q: Why do I get a 404 from the server when I refresh a page?
faqs.a: Because the browser asks the server for that path, and a single page app has only one real page. The server must send index.html for every path that is not an API route. Vite does it in development, and lesson 38 does it in production.

faqs.q: What is the Outlet for?
faqs.a: It marks where a layout route draws the matching child route, so shared parts like the header stay while only the page changes.

lessons.title: React Context and Custom Hooks: Sharing Auth State and Reusing Data Logic
lessons.description: Share the signed-in user with every component through context, extract data loading into a custom hook, and keep pages short.

content.text: Two problems appear as the app grows. First, many components need the same information, such as who is signed in, and passing it as props through every level (called *prop drilling*) is tedious and fragile. Second, the same loading logic gets copied from page to page. React answers the first with **context** and the second with **custom hooks**.
Context: share without passing props

items: `createContext(null)` makes a context. A **provider** component puts a value into it, and any component below the provider can read that value, however deep.
`AuthProvider` owns the state (`user` and `ready`) and offers them through `value`. `children` is whatever you wrap it around.

`useAuth()` is a **custom hook**: a function whose name starts with `use` that calls other hooks (`useContext` here). It reads the context and throws a clear error if you forget to wrap the app in the provider.
`ready` is `false` until the first attempt to sign in has finished. Pages can wait for it, so they do not flash a “signed out” screen to someone who is, in fact, signed in.

content.text: Here `AuthProvider` wraps `App`, inside `BrowserRouter` so that later code can navigate. As before, the effect signs in as the demo user. It is **temporary** and lives in one place now, rather than in every page, which makes it easy to remove in lesson 32.

Context is for values many components need and that change rarely, such as the user, a theme or the language. Putting fast-changing data (like what is in a text box) in context makes every component below it redraw. Keep that kind of state local.
Custom hooks: reuse logic

`useJobs` moves the list loading out of the page. It uses `useAuth` to wait for the sign-in, `useState` for the data, loading and error, and `useEffect` to fetch with an abort controller. It returns what a page needs: `jobs`, `loading`, `error`. A custom hook is just a function, and every component that calls it gets its **own** copy of the state. They share the *code*, not the *data*.

`useCallback` wraps `load` so that the function keeps the same identity between draws. That matters here because `load` appears in an effect's dependency array: a new function on every draw would make the effect run again and again.

Compare this page with lesson 29. It went from about 35 lines of effects and states to a single call, `useJobs()`. The page now says **what** to show; the hook knows **how** to get it. This is the main reason to write a custom hook: make the pages read like a description of the screen.
Your task

Add a `useDocumentTitle(title)` hook that sets `document.title` in an effect, and use it in both pages.
In React Developer Tools, find `AuthProvider` and its state.

items: Behaviour is the same as before, with less code in the pages.
`useAuth` explains the mistake when the provider is missing.

content.text: Summary

items: Context shares a value with all components below a provider; use it for rarely changing data like the user.
A custom hook is a `use...` function that reuses stateful logic. Each caller gets its own state.
Wrap functions in `useCallback` when they are dependencies of an effect.

faqs.q: When should I use context instead of props?
faqs.a: When many components at different depths need the same value, such as the current user, theme or language. For data used by one parent and its direct children, props are simpler and clearer.

faqs.q: Do two components using the same hook share state?
faqs.a: No. Each call to a hook creates its own state. A hook shares logic, not data. To share data, lift the state up or put it in context.

faqs.q: Why does a hook have to start with use?
faqs.a: It is a convention that tools rely on: the linter checks that hooks follow the rules (only call them at the top level of components and other hooks), and readers recognise them instantly.

lessons.title: CRUD in React: Create, Edit and Delete Jobs Through the API
lessons.description: Create, edit and delete jobs through the API, with delete confirmation and an optimistic status update that rolls back on failure.

content.text: Everything the person does on screen must now reach the database: add, change and delete. The three things to get right in a real app are the same three you have met on the server: **the happy path**, **the unhappy path** (show the server's field errors and failures), and **the waiting** (show that something is happening and prevent double clicks).
The hook now changes data

items: **`createJob`** waits for the server, which creates the real `id`, then puts the **saved** job at the top of the list. We do not invent an id on the client any more.

**`changeStatus`** is an **optimistic update**: it changes the screen at once, then sends the request. If the server refuses, it puts the old job back and shows an error. The screen feels instant, and the truth is restored if something goes wrong. Use this style for small, low-risk changes, and not for things like payments.
**`removeJob`** waits for the server first, and then removes the job from the list, since deleting is not something to guess.
All three are wrapped in `useCallback`, so they keep their identity. That will matter for performance in lesson 35.

content.text: A form that adds and edits

The same component now serves both purposes. `initial` fills the fields (empty for adding, the job for editing), `submitLabel` changes the button text, and `onSubmit` returns a **promise**. While it runs, `saving` is true: the button is disabled and says “Saving…”, which stops double submissions. If the server answers with field errors, `err.details` goes straight into the `errors` state, so a message appears under the right field. If it answers with another error, the message is shown below the button inside `role="alert"`, which screen readers announce.
Deleting uses `window.confirm` here. It is basic but accessible and quick to build. A custom dialog is nicer and is a good exercise. Before you delete anything, ask.
The edit page

The detail page shows the form filled with the job. The `key={job.updatedAt}` on `JobForm` makes React build a fresh form whenever the saved job changes, so the fields always show what the server holds. The save answer is stored back in `job`, and a “Saved.” note uses `role="status"`. After a delete it calls `navigate('/')` to go back to the list.
Treat the server as the truth. After an update, show what the server returned, not what you sent: the server may have trimmed a value or applied a default.
Handling failure like a professional

items: Never leave the person guessing: loading text, disabled buttons and clear messages.
Keep the failed input in the form so they can fix it, instead of clearing it.
Roll back optimistic changes when the server says no.
Do not show raw technical errors. The API's messages were written to be shown.

Stop the server and try to change a status. Does the old status come back, with an error message?
Submit the form with a company longer than 120 characters. Where does the message appear?

content.text: How to check it worked

items: New, edited and deleted jobs survive a reload.
A failed status change is rolled back with a message.
The submit button is disabled while saving.

content.text: Summary

items: Create and delete wait for the server; small changes can be optimistic with a rollback.
One form component serves adding and editing through `initial` and `onSubmit`.
Show saving, field errors and failures, and display what the server returned.

faqs.q: What is an optimistic update?
faqs.a: Changing the screen immediately, assuming the server will accept the change, and undoing it if the server refuses. It makes small actions feel instant. Avoid it where a wrong guess has real cost.

faqs.q: Why wait for the server when creating a job?
faqs.a: Because the server creates the real id and applies its own cleaning and defaults. Showing the saved version keeps the screen true to the data.

faqs.q: How do I stop double submissions?
faqs.a: Disable the submit button while the request is in progress, using a saving state, and show a "Saving…" label. The server can also protect itself with unique indexes or idempotent routes.
