lessons.title: Sign In and Register Pages with Protected Routes in React
lessons.description: Build real sign-in and registration screens, restore a session from a saved token, protect private pages, handle expired tokens, and sign out.

content.text: It is time to remove the temporary demo login from lessons 28 to 31 and let real people create accounts. This lesson connects the pieces from the back end (register, login, `/auth/me`, 401 answers) to React: pages for signing in and registering, a way to **restore a session** after a refresh, **protected routes**, and a clean **sign out**.
The auth context, for real

items: **On first load**, if a token is saved, it asks the server `GET /api/auth/me`. A valid answer restores the user; an error removes the bad token. Only then is `ready` set to `true`. A saved token is a *claim*, so the server must confirm it.
**`signIn` and `register`** call the API, save the token with `setToken`, and set `user`.
**`signOut`** deletes the token and clears the user. Because the token is stateless, “signing out” only forgets it on this device. The server has no session to end.

**A listener for `jt:unauthorized`.** If any request later gets a `401` (an expired token, for instance), the API helper fires this event and the context signs the person out, so they land on the login page with no extra code in any page.

content.text: Look at the 401 branch in `api()`. It dispatches the event only when a token existed and the request was not the login itself, because a wrong password on the login form is not an expired session.
Protecting pages

`ProtectedRoute` is a layout route. It waits while `ready` is false, redirects to `/login` when there is no user, and otherwise draws `<Outlet />`, the protected page. `<Navigate replace state={{ from }} />` remembers where the person wanted to go, so after signing in we can send them there. `replace` avoids leaving the redirect in the back-button history.

Hiding screens in React is **user experience, not security**. Anyone can open the browser tools and change what the page shows. The real protection is the server, which checks the token and the owner on every request (lessons 21 and 22).
The two forms

items: Use the right **input types and `autoComplete`** values (`email`, `current-password`, `new-password`). Password managers and phone keyboards rely on them, and they make signing in much easier.
If someone is already signed in and opens `/login`, `<Navigate to="/" />` sends them to the app.
The login page navigates to `location.state?.from`, then falls back to `/`.
Registration shows the server's field errors (`err.details`) under each field, using the same pattern as the job form.
Both disable the button while waiting, and show failures in a `role="alert"` paragraph.

content.text: The header now shows either the app link or the sign-in links, and, when signed in, the person's name and a **Sign out** button. Names come from the server and are drawn through JSX, which escapes them automatically. Never insert user-written text with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`: it is the way cross-site scripting happens in React apps.
Your task

items: Delete any saved `jt_token` from `localStorage` (Application tab) and open the app. You should land on the login page.
Create an account on the register page. Try a short password and a repeated email first.
Sign out, then try to open `/` directly. You are redirected, then returned after signing in.
In the browser tools, change the saved token to garbage and reload. What happens?

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Registration and login work and show field errors.
A protected page redirects signed-out visitors and returns them after login.
A bad or expired token signs the person out.

content.text: Summary

items: Restore sessions by asking the server who the saved token belongs to.
`ProtectedRoute` redirects visitors who are not signed in. This is a convenience; the server enforces the rules.
A global `401` event signs the person out in one place.

faqs.q: Where should I store the JWT in the browser?
faqs.a: localStorage is simple and common, but scripts on the page can read it, so any XSS bug could steal it. An httpOnly cookie cannot be read by scripts but needs CSRF protection. Pick one with the trade-off in mind; lesson 40 lists cookies as a next step.

faqs.q: How do I sign out when the token is stateless?
faqs.a: You forget the token on the client. The server cannot end it earlier unless you keep a list of revoked tokens, which most small apps do not need if tokens expire soon.

faqs.q: Is a protected route in React real security?
faqs.a: No. It only hides screens. A person can still call your API directly, so the server must check the token and the owner on every request.

lessons.title: A React Dashboard: Statistics, Filters and Pagination Stored in the URL
lessons.description: Show the API statistics, add search, status filter and sorting, paginate, and keep all of it in the URL so a page can be shared, bookmarked and reloaded.

content.text: The API can already search, filter, sort, paginate and count. This lesson gives it a face. The interesting design decision is **where the state lives**. Instead of keeping the search text and page number in component state, we keep them in the **address bar**: `/?status=applied&q=bank&page=2`. That gives you three things for free: the back button works, reloading keeps your place, and the person can bookmark or share a view.
The hook follows the URL

items: It takes `{ q, status, sort, page, limit }` and builds the query string with `URLSearchParams`, which also takes care of encoding special characters.

The effect depends on `query` (a string) and `version` (a number). When the filters change, the query changes and the effect fetches again. When data changes (a job is added, deleted or moved), `reload()` increases `version`, which runs the effect again so the list **and the statistics** refresh.

It loads the list and the statistics together with `Promise.all`, and aborts the old requests in the cleanup. That is what prevents the classic search bug: you type `ba` then `bank`, and the slower first answer arrives last and overwrites the right one.

content.text: The page reads the URL

`useSearchParams()` works like `useState` for the query string: it returns the current parameters and a function to change them. The page reads `q`, `status`, `sort` and `page` from it, with sensible defaults, and hands them to `useJobs`. `setFilter` copies the current parameters, applies the change, and **drops `page`**. If you are on page 4 and choose a status with only two pages of results, staying on page 4 would show nothing. `replace: true` replaces the current history entry rather than adding one, so typing in the search box does not create dozens of back-button steps.
Small, focused components

import { STATUSES } from './JobCard.jsx'; // The filters live in the URL (/?status=applied&q=bank), so a page can be bookmarked, shared and reloaded. export default function Filters({ q, status, sort, onChange }) { return (
e.preventDefault()}>
onChange({ q: e.target.value })} />
); }

items: **`StatsBar`** shows the numbers from `/api/jobs/stats`. `interviewRate` can be `null` (lesson 19), and the bar shows “–” instead of a number that would mean nothing. It sits inside `<section aria-label=...>` so screen readers can find it.
**`Filters`** is a `role="search"` form with labelled controls. It does not own any state: it receives the values and a single `onChange`, so it is easy to reuse and test.
**`Pagination`** disables Previous and Next at the ends and announces the page with `aria-live="polite"`.

content.text: Notice the “no results” messages. “No job matches these filters” and “No jobs yet” are different situations that need different words, so the code distinguishes them with a `filtered` flag. The count line also changes between “1 job” and “3 jobs”. Details like this are what make a screen feel finished.

The search box in this lesson sends a request on every keystroke. It works, because the aborted requests keep the answers in order, but it makes more requests than needed. Lesson 35 adds a **debounce** to fix that.

faqs.q: Why keep filters in the URL instead of in state?
faqs.a: The back button, reload, bookmarks and shared links all work for free, and the URL always shows the exact view. State kept in a component is lost on reload.

faqs.q: Why reset the page when a filter changes?
faqs.a: The new result set may have fewer pages. If you stay on page 4 of a result that only has 2, the screen would be empty and confusing.

faqs.q: What is the problem with searching on every keystroke?
faqs.a: It sends many requests, and answers can arrive out of order. Aborting old requests solves the ordering, and a debounce (lesson 35) reduces the number of requests.

lessons.title: Responsive Styling and Accessibility: Mobile First CSS, Focus, Contrast and Dark Mode
lessons.description: Style the app for phones first, make it keyboard friendly, respect reduced motion and dark mode, and move focus after page changes.

content.text: Many of the people using a job tracker use it on a phone, often on a slow connection, sometimes with large text or a screen reader, and sometimes in a dim room. Design for them first and the app is better for everyone. This lesson replaces the basic styles with a responsive, accessible stylesheet and adds three small changes to the layout.
Mobile first

**Mobile first** means the base rules are written for a narrow screen, and `@media (min-width: 600px)` blocks *add* room for bigger ones. The form is one column on a phone and two on a tablet. The statistics are two columns, then four, then seven. This is easier than the other way round, and phones get the least CSS to process.

items: **Flexible units and layout.** `grid` with `1fr` columns, `flex-wrap`, `max-width` and no fixed widths mean nothing sticks out of a 390 px screen. Test by opening the browser tools and choosing a phone size. The page must never scroll sideways.
**Touch targets.** Buttons and inputs have `min-height: 44px`, because fingers are less precise than a mouse pointer.
**Logical properties** such as `margin-inline-start` and `inset-inline-start` flip automatically for right-to-left languages like Arabic, so the same CSS serves them.

content.text: Colour, contrast and dark mode

Text needs enough contrast against its background to be read in sunlight and by people with low vision. The muted text colour was darkened from the first version for that reason, and the status badges pair dark text with a light background. A quick check is to use the contrast checker in the browser tools. The `prefers-color-scheme: dark` block swaps the custom properties when the device is set to dark mode, so the whole interface follows with a few lines, because every colour comes from a variable.

Never use colour alone to carry meaning. The status badges also contain the **word** (`applied`, `offer`), and invalid fields have a thicker border *and* a text message, so people who cannot tell the colours apart lose nothing.
Focus and keyboard use

items: `:focus-visible` draws a clear outline for keyboard users and stays out of the way for mouse users. **Never** remove the outline without replacing it.
A **skip link** (“Skip to content”) is the first thing a keyboard user can reach. It is hidden above the page until it gets focus. It lets them jump past the header on every page.
After a page change in a single page app, nothing tells a screen reader that the page changed. The layout now **moves focus to `<main>`** when the address changes, so the new content is read out.

content.text: `tabIndex={-1}` makes `main` focusable by code without adding it to the Tab order, and `focus({ preventScroll: true })` avoids the page jumping. Together with `id="main"` they give the skip link a target.
Respect the person's settings

The last rule in the stylesheet switches off animations and transitions when the device asks for **reduced motion**. Some people feel dizzy or sick from movement on screen. The same attention applies to text size: use `rem` or relative sizes so the browser's font-size setting works.
A quick accessibility test you can do today

items: Put the mouse away and do the whole flow with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter and the arrow keys.
Zoom the page to 200 percent. Nothing should overlap or be cut off.
Turn on a screen reader (VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, TalkBack on Android, NVDA on Windows) and listen to one page.
Run the Lighthouse accessibility audit in Chrome and fix what it reports.

faqs.q: What does mobile first mean?
faqs.a: You write the default styles for a small screen and use min-width media queries to add layout for larger ones. The smallest, simplest layout is the base, and bigger screens add to it.

faqs.q: How big should buttons be on a phone?
faqs.a: Aim for about 44 by 44 CSS pixels, which is a widely used guideline for touch targets, so people can tap them without hitting the wrong thing.

faqs.q: Why move focus to main after a page change?
faqs.a: In a single page app the browser does not reload, so screen readers get no signal that a new page appeared. Moving focus to the main content announces it and puts keyboard users in the right place.

lessons.title: React Performance: memo, Debounce and Code Splitting with lazy
lessons.description: Stop unnecessary redraws with memo, cut requests with a debounce hook, and shrink the first download by loading pages only when needed.

content.text: Performance advice often starts with the wrong lesson: “optimise everything”. The right order is to **measure first**, fix what is slow, and leave the rest alone. Most small apps are fast without any tricks. But three techniques are cheap, safe and worth knowing, because they solve problems you will meet: unnecessary redraws, too many requests, and a big first download.
1. Debounce: wait until typing stops

`useDebounce(value, delay)` returns a copy of `value` that only changes after the original has stopped changing for `delay` milliseconds. Each change starts a timer, and the cleanup function cancels the previous one, so only the last one fires. Typing “bank” sends one request instead of four.

The search box now shows what you type **at once** from local `text` state, so typing never feels laggy, and only the debounced value is passed up, which updates the URL and triggers the request. The second effect handles the other direction: if the address changes by itself (the back button, “clear filters”), the box follows it. Read the two effects carefully: they are written so they cannot overwrite what you are typing.
2. memo: skip redraws that would change nothing

When a parent component draws again, all its children draw again too, even if their props are the same. For a handful of cards that is nothing. For fifty cards that each contain a `<select>`, it adds up. `memo(JobCard)` tells React to skip drawing a card when its props are **identical to last time**.

This only works if the props really are the same. That is why earlier lessons took care of two things. Jobs are replaced only when they change (the spread in `changeStatus`, never mutation), so an unchanged `job` object is the same reference. And `changeStatus` is wrapped in `useCallback`, so its identity is stable. If the page passed a new inline function such as `onStatusChange={(id, s) => ...}` on each draw, `memo` would do nothing. Performance work is often just consistency.

Do not wrap everything in `memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` “just in case”. Each one has a cost and makes code harder to read. Use them when you have measured a slow screen (React Developer Tools has a Profiler), or, as here, where a list of many similar items is clearly the hot spot.
3. Code splitting: download less at the start

A single bundle contains the code of every page, so the person downloads the registration form even if they only wanted to sign in. `lazy(() => import('./pages/X.jsx'))` tells the bundler to put that page in its **own file**, which is fetched the first time the route is needed. `<Suspense fallback=...>` shows something while it loads. The build output shows the result: instead of one large file you will see a small file per page.
Measure the result

items: Run `npm run build` in `client` and compare the list of files and their sizes before and after.
In the browser's Network tab, throttle to “Slow 3G” and reload the login page. Only the login code should be fetched.
In the Performance and Lighthouse panels you will see numbers such as first paint. Treat them as a guide, not a score to chase.

Open React Developer Tools, enable “Highlight updates when components render”, and change one status. With `memo`, only one card flashes.
Build the client and note how many JavaScript files appear. Open the login page and see which are loaded.

faqs.q: Should I use memo, useMemo and useCallback everywhere?
faqs.a: No. They cost memory and make code harder to read. Use them when a profiler shows a real slowdown, or for a long list of identical items as in this lesson.

faqs.q: What does a debounce do?
faqs.a: It waits until a value stops changing for a short time before acting on it. For a search box it turns many keystrokes into one request.

faqs.q: What is code splitting?
faqs.a: Building your JavaScript into several files so that the browser only downloads the code for the page it needs. React.lazy and dynamic import() do it for routes.

lessons.title: File Upload with Multer and React: Attach a Resume to a Job Safely
lessons.description: Accept PDF and Word files with multer, check size, type and file signature, store a random name, and let the owner download it.

content.text: People often want to keep the resume they sent with each application. File upload is a feature that looks simple and hides several security traps, because you are letting strangers put files on your server. This lesson builds it carefully: only the owner can attach or read a file, only PDF and Word files are accepted, the size is limited, and the name on disk is never chosen by the client.
How an upload travels

A browser sends a file in a request with the content type `multipart/form-data`: a body made of parts, one for each field, each with its own headers. `express.json()` does not understand it, so we use **multer**, a middleware that reads the parts, saves the file and puts the details in `req.file`. The other form fields end up in `req.body`.
The upload middleware

items: **Limits**: `fileSize` is 2 MB and `files` is 1. Without a size limit, one visitor could fill your disk.

**A random file name** made with `crypto.randomBytes(16)`. The client's file name is never used as a path. A name such as `../../etc/passwd` or `evil.js` cannot clash with another file or leave the folder. We keep the original name only as text to show the person.
**`fileFilter`** accepts only the extensions `.pdf`, `.doc` and `.docx`.

**The magic bytes check.** The extension and the type the browser reports are claims made by the client, and a person can rename any file to `.pdf`. `looksLikeAllowedFile` reads the first bytes of the saved file: a PDF starts with `%PDF-`, a `.docx` is a zip and starts with `PK`, an old `.doc` has its own signature. A file that does not match is deleted.
**`removeFile`** only deletes names matching the exact pattern we generate, so it can never be tricked into deleting another file.

content.text: Never serve uploaded files from a public folder with their stored names, and never allow types such as `.html`, `.svg` or `.js`: a browser that opens them can run the code in the context of your site. Here every download goes through a route that checks ownership and sends the file as an attachment.
The data and the controller

The file stays on disk and only its details go in MongoDB, in a small embedded `resume` object. The `toJSON` transform shows the client only `name`, `size` and `uploadedAt`. It hides `storedName`, the real file name.

items: **`ownJob`** finds the job **with the owner filter** from lesson 22. All three routes use it, so another person's job gives a `404`, whatever they try.
**Upload** checks the signature, deletes the old file if there is one, saves the new details, and, if anything fails, removes the new file so that no orphan stays on disk (the `catch` block).
**Download** uses `res.download(path, originalName)`, which sets `Content-Disposition: attachment` so the browser saves the file with the person's own file name.
**Delete** removes the file and the details together. Deleting the whole job also removes its file (see `controllers/jobs.js` in this lesson).

content.text: `upload.single('resume')` is **route middleware** in front of the handler, as lesson 10 described: the string must match the form field name used by the client. Errors from multer, such as a file that is too large, are turned into friendly answers by the error handler (`413` for size, `400` for the rest).
The React side

`api()` now accepts a `FormData` body and **does not set** the `Content-Type` header. The browser sets it and adds the *boundary* that separates the parts. If you set it yourself, the boundary is missing and the upload fails. `downloadFile` exists because a plain `<a href>` cannot send our `Authorization` header: it fetches the file with the token and saves it from memory.

The component checks the size on the client first (a courtesy that saves the upload time), then sends the file with `new FormData()` and `append('resume', file)`. `e.target.value = ''` resets the input so that choosing the same file twice still fires a change. The server checks everything again, because the client can be bypassed.
Your task

items: Run `npm install` in `server` (adds `multer`), and attach a PDF to a job on its detail page. Download it again.
Rename a text file to `fake.pdf` and try to upload it. Read the message.
Try a file larger than 2 MB, and a `.exe` file.
Look in `server/uploads`. What are the files called? Delete the job and check that its file is gone.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A real PDF is accepted and downloads with its original name.
A fake PDF, a big file and a wrong type are refused with clear messages.
A second user cannot download the first user's file.

content.text: Summary

items: Use multer for `multipart/form-data`; limit size and count; filter by extension.
Check the file's first bytes, store it under a random name, and serve it only through an owner-checked route.
In React send a `FormData` and let the browser set the content type.

faqs.q: Why check the first bytes of a file?
faqs.a: The file name and the type reported by the browser are controlled by the sender. The first bytes (the signature) are much harder to fake while keeping a useful file, so they give a stronger check that a PDF really is a PDF.

faqs.q: Why not use the original file name on the server?
faqs.a: It can contain path tricks such as ../, clash with existing files, or have a dangerous extension. A random generated name avoids all of that. Keep the original name as text only, to show people.

faqs.q: Why does my React upload fail with a missing boundary error?
faqs.a: You set the Content-Type header yourself. For FormData let the browser set it, because it adds the boundary string that separates the parts of the body.

lessons.title: Production-Ready Express: Structured Logs, Graceful Shutdown, Compression and Indexes
lessons.description: Prepare the server for the real world: JSON logs without secrets, clean shutdown, a real health check, gzip, and building indexes on purpose.

content.text: Code that works on your laptop is not yet code that is ready for real visitors. Production needs things that are easy to forget because nothing looks broken without them: logs you can search when something goes wrong, a server that stops cleanly instead of cutting people off mid-request, a health check that tells the truth, and a database that has the right indexes. This lesson adds all of them with small changes.
1. Logs you can read at 3 a.m.

In development a person reads the terminal, so a readable line is best. In production the logs are collected and searched by tools, so **one JSON object per line** (with `time`, `level`, `message` and fields) is best: you can filter by status code or find slow requests with a search. The tiny logger does both, chosen by `NODE_ENV`.

items: It logs the **path only** (`req.path`), not the full URL. A query string can contain private information, such as a search for a person's name.
It never logs the **body or the headers**. They contain passwords and the `Authorization` token, and logs are copied around far more freely than databases are.
It records the status and the time in milliseconds, which is enough to find slow and failing routes.

content.text: 2. Shutting down politely

When you deploy a new version, the process manager sends the old process a `SIGTERM` signal. If the program simply dies, any requests being answered at that moment fail. The handler here does it properly: it **stops accepting new connections and waits for the current ones to finish** (`server.close`), closes the database connection, and exits. A timer forces exit after 10 seconds so a stuck connection cannot block a deploy. `unhandledRejection` logs promises that nobody caught and exits, since the process may be in a bad state and the process manager will start a fresh one.
3. A health check that tells the truth

`/api/health` now answers `503` when the database is not connected, and `200` when it is, together with the uptime. Load balancers, uptime monitors and your own deploy script use it to decide whether to send traffic. A health check that always says “OK” is worse than none.

`compression()` gzips text responses (JSON, HTML, JavaScript), which are often a quarter of their original size. That matters on mobile connections. In many setups nginx does it instead; use one or the other.
4. Build indexes on purpose

Mongoose creates the indexes described in your schemas when the app starts (`autoIndex`). On a small database that is fine. On a large one, building an index can be slow and heavy, and you do not want it to happen every time a server restarts. So in production `autoIndex` is off, and you run the sync **deliberately** after a deploy that changed an index.

`syncIndexes()` creates missing indexes and removes ones that are no longer in the schema. It is the same function that fixed the test flakiness in lesson 24. Our `deploy.sh` in lesson 39 runs it for you.

Monitoring is the other half of production. Even a simple uptime check that calls `/api/health` every minute and emails you is far better than finding out from a visitor. Many free and paid services do this; check what suits your budget.
Your task

items: Run `npm install` in `server` (adds `compression`). Start with `NODE_ENV=production` and a long `JWT_SECRET` and look at the JSON log lines.
Press Ctrl + C while a request is running (add a one second delay to a route to test). Watch the shutdown messages.
Stop MongoDB and call `/api/health`. You should get `503`.
Run `npm run indexes` and read what it prints.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: In production mode each log line is one JSON object with no passwords or tokens.
Ctrl + C prints the shutdown messages and exits with code 0.
The health check answers 503 without a database.

content.text: Summary

items: Log JSON in production, only path, status and timing, never secrets.
Handle `SIGTERM`: finish requests, close the database, then exit.
Make health checks honest, compress text, and build indexes deliberately.

faqs.q: Why log JSON in production?
faqs.a: Log tools can search and filter structured fields such as status and duration, which is much harder with free text lines. Keep readable lines for development.

faqs.q: What is a graceful shutdown?
faqs.a: Stopping a server in a way that lets requests that are already being answered finish, closing database connections cleanly, and only then exiting. It avoids errors for people during a deploy.

faqs.q: Why turn autoIndex off in production?
faqs.a: Building indexes on a large collection can be slow and heavy, and it should not happen on every restart. Run syncIndexes yourself after a deploy that changes indexes.

lessons.title: Build for Production and Serve the React App from Express
lessons.description: Create the optimised React build, let Express serve it with correct caching, send index.html for client-side routes, and keep unknown API paths as JSON 404.

content.text: In development you ran two servers: Vite for the screens and Express for the API. In production the simplest setup runs **one**. `npm run build` turns your React source into a small set of static files, and Express serves those files and the API from the same address. That removes CORS from the picture, needs only one process to manage, and means the token and the pages share an origin.
What the build does

`vite build` bundles your JSX and CSS into plain JavaScript and CSS files in `client/dist`, minified, with a hash in each file name (`assets/index-BBRz7k9l.js`). The hash changes whenever the content changes. That detail drives the caching rules below.
Serving the build

items: **The folder.** `client/dist` is found relative to this file, or from `CLIENT_DIST`. If it does not exist (for example in tests or in development), nothing is served and the API still works.

**Caching.** Files in `/assets` have the hash in their name, so they can never change under the same name. They get `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, a year. `index.html` must **never** be cached: it points at the current hashed files, and an old cached copy would point at files you have deleted. It gets `no-cache`.

**The fallback.** React Router draws pages like `/jobs/123` in the browser, but the server has no such file. `app.get(/^\/(?!api\/).*/, ...)` answers any GET that does not start with `/api/` with `index.html`, so reloading or sharing a deep link works.
**API 404s.** `app.use('/api', notFound)` comes *before* the fallback. An unknown API path must be a JSON `404`, and not a copy of the home page, which would confuse scripts and hide bugs.

content.text: Order again: API routes, then `/api` 404, then static files, then the fallback, then the general 404 and the error handler. Reading the file top to bottom should match the order a request is tried.
Security headers and the build

`helmet()` sets a Content Security Policy that only allows scripts from your own site. The Vite build loads its code from files, not inline scripts, so it works under that policy. If you later add something like an analytics script or fonts from another site, you will have to allow them in the policy on purpose. That is the policy doing its job.
Run it like production

From the project root: `npm run build` creates `client/dist`, and `npm start` starts the server. With `NODE_ENV=production` and a real `JWT_SECRET` set in `server/.env`, open `http://localhost:5000` and use the whole app from that single port. This is exactly what the server will do after deployment, so it is the best test before you deploy.
Your task

items: Run `npm run build` at the project root. Look at the `client/dist/assets` folder and the file sizes.
Start only the server (`npm start`) and open `http://localhost:5000`. Sign in and use the app.
Reload on a deep link such as `/jobs/<an id>`. It should work.
Open `/api/nothing` and `/nothing` and compare the answers.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The app works from port 5000 with no Vite running.
Deep links survive a reload.
`/api/nothing` is JSON 404, and `/nothing` shows the React 404 page.

content.text: Summary

items: `vite build` creates hashed static files; Express serves them with year-long caching for `/assets` and none for `index.html`.
Send `index.html` for every non-API GET so client-side routes work.
Keep the order: API, API 404, static, fallback, error handler.

faqs.q: Why is index.html not cached but assets are?
faqs.a: Asset file names contain a hash of their content, so a new version has a new name and can be cached for a year. index.html has a fixed name and points at the current assets, so it must be fetched fresh or visitors could get stale pages.

faqs.q: Do I need nginx if Express serves the files?
faqs.a: Not strictly. nginx in front is still useful for HTTPS, large uploads, compression and serving many sites on one server, which is what lesson 39 sets up.

faqs.q: Why serve the API and the React app from one origin?
faqs.a: The browser then sees a single origin, so no CORS settings are needed, and there is one thing to deploy and monitor. Large teams sometimes split them for scaling reasons.

lessons.title: Deploy a MERN App to a VPS with pm2, nginx and HTTPS (Let's Encrypt)
lessons.description: Put the Job Tracker on a Linux server: environment file, pm2 process manager, nginx reverse proxy, free HTTPS certificate, and a repeatable deploy script.

content.text: Everything so far runs on your own computer. To let other people use it, the app needs a computer that is always on and reachable. This lesson uses a **VPS** (a small rented Linux server, offered by many hosting companies) with the classic setup that many production sites still use: **pm2** keeps Node.js running, **nginx** receives visitors and talks to it, and **Let's Encrypt** provides a free HTTPS certificate. The files in this lesson's zip are templates: replace the example domain and paths with yours.

Other options exist, such as platform services that deploy from Git for you. They are convenient, and prices and features change often, so check their sites. Knowing the manual way means you understand what those services do for you.
The pieces

items: **A domain name** pointing to the server's IP address (an `A` record in your DNS settings).
**Node.js 20+, nginx, git and certbot** installed on the server, and **pm2** (`npm install -g pm2`).
**MongoDB Atlas** for the database, with the server's IP address allowed in Network Access, and a database user limited to this one database.
**A non-root user** for running the app, and a firewall that opens only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS.

content.text: The environment file

# Copy to server/.env on the server and fill it in. This file is a list of names only: never put real secrets in Git.
NODE_ENV=production
PORT=5000
TRUST_PROXY=1
# Your Atlas connection string (create a database user with read/write on this one database only)
MONGODB_URI=mongodb+srv://USER:PASSWORD@cluster0.xxxxx.mongodb.net/job_tracker
# 48 random bytes:  node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(48).toString('hex'))"
JWT_SECRET=
JWT_EXPIRES_IN=7d
# The public address of the site (only needed if the React app is served from a different origin)
CLIENT_ORIGIN=https://jobtracker.example.com

On the server, copy it to `server/.env` and fill it in. `NODE_ENV=production` turns on the production behaviour from lesson 37 (JSON logs, indexes off). `TRUST_PROXY=1` is essential behind nginx (lesson 23). Create the secret with the command in the comment, and run `chmod 600 server/.env` so only your user can read it. The real file never goes into Git.
pm2: keep the app running

If the Node.js process crashes, nothing restarts it by default. **pm2** does: it starts the app, restarts it after a crash or when it uses too much memory, keeps the logs (`pm2 logs`), and with `pm2 startup` plus `pm2 save` starts it again after a server reboot. `kill_timeout` gives the graceful shutdown from lesson 37 time to finish. The file ends in `.cjs` because pm2 reads it as a classic module, even though the app itself uses ES modules.
nginx: the front door

nginx listens on ports 80 and 443 and **proxies** requests to your app on port 5000. The `X-Forwarded-*` headers tell Express the real visitor IP address and whether the connection was HTTPS. `client_max_body_size 3m` matters for our resume uploads: nginx's default is 1 MB and it would answer `413` before your app saw the request. After changing nginx, always run `sudo nginx -t` to check the file, then `sudo systemctl reload nginx`.

For HTTPS, `sudo certbot --nginx -d your-domain` gets a free certificate from Let's Encrypt, edits the nginx file to use it, adds a redirect from HTTP to HTTPS, and sets up automatic renewal. Test that renewal works with `sudo certbot renew --dry-run`.
A repeatable deploy

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run on the server from the project folder:  bash deploy/deploy.sh
set -euo pipefail

git pull --ff-only
npm install --prefix server --omit=dev
npm install --prefix client            # the build needs the dev tools (Vite)
npm run build --prefix client
(cd server && node scripts/sync-indexes.js)
pm2 startOrReload deploy/ecosystem.config.cjs --env production
pm2 save
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/health && echo "  <- healthy"

The script runs, in order: pull the latest code (`--ff-only` refuses to make an unexpected merge), install server packages without development tools, install client packages and build the React app, sync the database indexes, reload pm2, and finally call the health check. `set -euo pipefail` stops at the first error, so a failed build never reaches “reload”. `pm2 startOrReload` replaces the process without a long gap.

# Deploying the Job Tracker to a VPS

You need: a small Linux server (Ubuntu), a domain name pointing at its IP address, and a MongoDB Atlas cluster.

## One time

1. Create a non-root user, enable the firewall (`ufw allow OpenSSH`, `ufw allow 'Nginx Full'`, `ufw enable`) and update the system.
2. Install Node.js 20+, nginx, git, certbot and pm2 (`npm install -g pm2`).
3. In Atlas: Network Access must allow your server's IP address. Create a database user that can read and write only the `job_tracker` database.
4. `git clone` your repository to `/var/www/job-tracker`.
5. `cp server/.env.production.example server/.env` and fill in every value. Then `chmod 600 server/.env`.
6. Copy `deploy/nginx.conf` into `/etc/nginx/sites-available/`, change the domain, link it into `sites-enabled`, run `sudo nginx -t` and reload nginx.
7. `sudo certbot --nginx -d your-domain` for HTTPS.
8. `pm2 startup` and run the command it prints, so the app starts after a reboot.

## Every release

`bash deploy/deploy.sh`

It pulls the code, installs packages, builds the React app, syncs MongoDB indexes, reloads pm2 and checks `/api/health`.

## If something is wrong

| Symptom | Look at |
|---|---|
| 502 Bad Gateway | `pm2 logs job-tracker`: the app is not running or the port is not 5000 |
| App starts then exits | the first log line: usually a missing variable in `.env` or Atlas refusing your IP |
| Login works but you are signed out at once | `TRUST_PROXY=1` missing or `JWT_SECRET` changed |
| Upload answers 413 | `client_max_body_size` in nginx |
| Page refresh shows JSON "No route" | the React build is missing: run `npm run build --prefix client` |

## Backups

Turn on Atlas backups (or run `mongodump` on a schedule) and copy `server/uploads/` somewhere safe. Uploaded files are not in MongoDB.

The file above has the one-time steps and a troubleshooting table. The symptoms in it are the ones people actually meet: a `502` (the app is not running), a crash at start (usually a missing variable or Atlas refusing your IP), an upload `413` (nginx limit), and being signed out immediately (a missing `TRUST_PROXY` or a changed secret).

Back up two things: the database (turn on Atlas backups, or run `mongodump` on a schedule) and the `server/uploads` folder. Uploaded files are not in MongoDB. A backup you have never restored is only a hope: try a restore once.
Your task

items: Read `docs/DEPLOY.md` and tick off each one-time step for your own server (you can do this on any small test server).
Replace `jobtracker.example.com` with your domain in `deploy/nginx.conf`.
Run the deploy steps by hand once, then with `bash deploy/deploy.sh`.
After deploying, stop the app with `pm2 stop job-tracker`, visit the site (what do you see?), and start it again.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `https://your-domain/api/health` answers `ok: true`.
The site works over HTTPS, and HTTP redirects to it.
After `sudo reboot`, the app comes back by itself.

content.text: Summary

items: pm2 keeps Node.js running; nginx handles HTTPS and large uploads; Atlas holds the data.
Set `NODE_ENV=production` and `TRUST_PROXY=1`; keep `.env` out of Git with strict permissions.
Script the deploy and finish with a health check; back up the database and the uploads folder.

faqs.q: Do I need nginx and pm2, or can I use a hosting platform?
faqs.a: Hosting platforms that deploy from Git do the same jobs for you and are quicker to start with. Doing it by hand on a VPS teaches what those platforms automate and gives you full control. Compare current prices and limits on their sites.

faqs.q: Why do I get 502 Bad Gateway?
faqs.a: nginx could not reach your app. Check that it is running (pm2 status), that it listens on the port in the nginx file, and read pm2 logs for the first error, often a missing environment variable.

faqs.q: How do I renew the HTTPS certificate?
faqs.a: Certbot sets up automatic renewal when you install the certificate. Check it with certbot renew --dry-run, and make sure the nginx server name still matches your domain.

lessons.description: A final production checklist, the mistakes that catch most beginners, and eight ideas to extend the Job Tracker with what you learned.

content.text: You have built and deployed a complete full stack application: a React front end, an Express API, a MongoDB database, sign-in, file uploads and a production server. This last lesson turns what you did into habits. It has a checklist you can reuse on every project, a list of the mistakes that most often catch people, and a plan for what to build next.
The checklist

# Before you call it finished

## Security
- [ ] `.env` is in `.gitignore` and was never committed (check with `git log --all -- server/.env`)
- [ ] `JWT_SECRET` is long, random and different from development
- [ ] Every private route uses `protect`, and every query includes the signed-in user's id
- [ ] Passwords are hashed; the hash is never returned
- [ ] Uploads: type, size and file signature are checked, names are random
- [ ] Rate limit on sign-in and sign-up; helmet on; CORS lists only your own site

## Quality
- [ ] `npm test` passes in `server/`
- [ ] The app works on a phone-sized screen and with the keyboard only
- [ ] Empty, loading and error states exist for every list and form

## Production
- [ ] HTTPS works and HTTP redirects to it
- [ ] `/api/health` is watched by an uptime monitor
- [ ] Database backups are on and you have restored one at least once
- [ ] Logs are readable with `pm2 logs`, and contain no passwords or tokens

Run through it before you share any app. A few lines deserve a comment. “`.env` was never committed” must be checked in the Git **history**, not only in the current files, because a secret committed once stays in history even after you delete the file. If it ever was, change the secret. “Every query includes the signed-in user's id” is the single most valuable security habit in the course. And “you have restored a backup at least once” turns a hope into a plan.
Mistakes that catch almost everyone

items: **Forgetting `await`**, and then wondering why a value is `Promise { <pending> }` or why data is missing.
**Mutating state** in React (changing an array or object in place) so the screen does not update.
**Missing dependencies** in `useEffect`, which cause stale data, or **new functions in dependencies**, which cause endless loops.
**Trusting the client**: no validation on the server, or taking the user id from the request body.
**Route order** in Express: `/:id` before `/stats`.
**Secrets in Git**, or a database open to the whole internet.
**No loading, empty or error states**, so a slow connection looks like a broken app.
**Testing only the happy path.** Bad input, no token and someone else's data are where the bugs are.

content.text: Where each lesson's idea shows up again

It helps to see the course as a few ideas used repeatedly, rather than forty topics. **A request has a shape** (lessons 1, 5, 9). **Middleware is a pipeline** (10, 12, 22, 23, 36). **Never trust input** (12, 17, 18, 23, 36). **Data belongs to someone** (20, 22, 36). **State is replaced, not edited** (26, 31, 33). **Effects have cleanups** (28, 33, 35). **The URL is state** (29, 33). **Failure needs a design** (12, 28, 31, 37). When you meet a new library, look for these ideas and you will understand it quickly.
What to build next

# Where to go next

Each idea below uses only what you already built. Do them in this order.

1. **Interview dates**: add `interviewAt` to the Job model and show upcoming ones first on the dashboard.
2. **Delete my account**: a route that deletes the user, all of their jobs and their uploaded files.
3. **Refresh sign-in**: keep the token in an httpOnly cookie instead of localStorage (this needs `cookie-parser`, `credentials: 'include'` and a CSRF plan).
4. **Password reset by email**: a one-time token with an expiry, sent through an email provider.
5. **Tests for the React app**: Vitest and React Testing Library for `JobForm` and `Filters`.
6. **TypeScript**: convert the server first (the models give you the types), then the client.
7. **Docker**: one Dockerfile for the app and a compose file with MongoDB for local work.
8. **CI**: a GitHub Actions workflow that runs `npm test` and `npm run build` on every push.

Each idea uses only skills from this course, in a sensible order. **Interview dates** add a field, a sort and a screen. **Delete my account** is a good lesson in cleaning up related data and files, and many places require it by law. **Cookies instead of localStorage**, **password reset by email**, **tests for React**, **TypeScript**, **Docker** and **CI** are the usual next steps in professional work.

A project you can show is worth more than a list of courses. Put the Job Tracker on your own domain, write a short README with screenshots and what you learned, and keep improving it. Employers and clients look at working projects.
Your task

items: Run the checklist on your deployed app and tick every line honestly.
Pick one item from `docs/NEXT-STEPS.md` and build it, with a test.
Write a README for your repository: what it does, how to run it, and which parts you built yourself.
Teach one lesson of this course to someone else. Explaining is the best test of understanding.

faqs.q: What should I learn after the MERN stack?
faqs.a: Common next steps are TypeScript, automated tests for the front end, Docker, continuous integration, and a second framework such as Next.js. Choose by the jobs or projects you care about and look at real job adverts in your area.

faqs.q: How do I find out if a secret was ever committed to Git?
faqs.a: Search the history, for example with git log --all -- server/.env, or use a secret scanning tool. If a secret was committed, treat it as leaked: change it, even after removing the file.

faqs.q: Is the Job Tracker good enough to show in my portfolio?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is deployed, has a clear README with screenshots, and you can explain your choices (ownership checks, validation, indexes, uploads). Extend it with one feature of your own so it is clearly your work.
